anchor_text: your own science Exceeds, in that, the lists
summary: 'Science' here means knowledge or expertise, not natural science in the modern sense. 'Lists' means limits or boundaries — the outer boundary of what the Duke's own advice could add. The Duke is telling Escalus that Escalus's mastery of government already outstrips anything the Duke could teach him.
detail: 'Science' in the sense of organized knowledge or learning derives from Latin scientia; the meaning survived in English well into the seventeenth century before narrowing to experimental natural philosophy. 'Lists' in the sense of a boundary-fence (as in 'the lists' of a tournament field) was a standard Elizabethan figure for any outer limit. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'science' and 'list' (sb. 3), documents both usages across the canon.

anchor_text: you are as pregnant in As art and practice
summary: 'Pregnant' means well-informed, thoroughly versed, or quick to understand — nothing to do with physical pregnancy. The Duke says Escalus is as deeply steeped in the city's institutions and laws as any person living memory can recall.
detail: This sense of 'pregnant' — mentally full, ready, apt — is common in Shakespeare: 'pregnant in the question' (Othello 2.1), 'pregnant instrument' (Lear 2.1). It derives from Latin praegnans understood figuratively as 'full of matter.' OED s.v. 'pregnant' adj. 3 documents the sense 'mentally receptive, quick-witted; full of meaning.' The contrast with the modern pregnancy meaning is sharp enough to flip the sentence's sense for unprepared readers.

anchor_text: Heaven doth with us as we with torches do, Not light them for themselves
summary: The Duke uses an analogy: just as torches are lit not to burn for themselves but to give light to others, God gives virtues to people so those virtues can be used in the world. A talent kept private is no talent at all. The speech is the Duke's justification for forcing office on a reluctant Angelo.
detail: The torch-analogy is a Renaissance commonplace of civic humanism: the gifted man owes his gifts to the public. It echoes the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30, Geneva 1599), in which a servant who buries his talent rather than putting it to use is condemned. Shakespeare returns to the same metaphor in Sonnet 1 ('beauty's legacy') and in All's Well That Ends Well 1.1. The imagery running from TLN 34 through TLN 43 is a sustained economic conceit — talents, nature as a creditor, 'use' (interest) — anchored by the torch's simpler opening image.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Matthew 25:14-30 (Geneva 1599): the Parable of the Talents — the servant who buries rather than employs his master's money is cast into outer darkness.

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon

The Parable of the Talents parallel is mainstream and the economic conceit (talents, creditor, use) is explicit in TLN 34-43; the Sonnet 1 cross-reference is secondary but not misleading.

anchor_text: smallest scruple of her excellence But, like a thrifty goddess, she determines Herself the glory of a creditor, Both thanks and use
summary: 'Scruple' was a tiny unit of weight in an apothecary's measure — one-third of a dram — so 'the smallest scruple' means the tiniest fraction. 'Use' means interest on a loan: Nature is a careful lender who expects to be repaid both with gratitude and with the actual return (interest) on every gift she advances. The image sets up Angelo as nature's investment in public service.
detail: The financial conceit is central to the Duke's whole speech and to the play's larger concern with exchange and repayment — the word 'use' (usury, interest) recurs in debates about the law throughout Measure for Measure. A scruple as a weight equals 1.296 grams; as a unit of conscience or doubt it implies hesitation. Both senses are in play: nature lends down to the very last scruple of her gift and keeps account. 'Creditor' (TLN 41) continues the metaphor — nature as the lender who holds the ledger. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'scruple' and 'use' (interest).

sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. R. D. Eagleson (1986), s.v. 'scruple' (a small weight; a minute quantity) and 'use' (interest on money).

The weight-unit and financial glosses are sound; the detail's aside that the 'doubt/hesitation' sense of scruple is simultaneously active is a mild overreach since the passage is purely in the financial register, but the summary correctly foregrounds the weight meaning.

anchor_text: In our remove be thou at full ourself: Mortality and mercy in Vienna
summary: 'Remove' means departure or absence. The Duke is investing Angelo with the full powers of the sovereign: 'be thou at full ourself' means act as if you were me in every respect. This is the formal act of deputation — delegating the ruler's authority to a deputy — a serious constitutional act in Elizabethan theory, because the ruler's power came from God and could not simply be transferred like private property.
detail: The phrase 'Mortality and mercy' — the power of life and death, and the power of pardon — distills the two supreme prerogatives of a sovereign. To grant both to a deputy is to create a surrogate ruler. Elizabethan political theology held that the king's authority was divinely sanctioned (see divine right of kings); deputizing it fully to Angelo is the act the play will put under pressure, asking whether Angelo's 'precise' character can sustain its terrible weight. The royal 'we' ('our remove,' 'ourself') throughout the scene underscores that the Duke speaks with a formal majesty he is about to vacate.

sources.name: Lever, Arden Measure for Measure
sources.citation: J. W. Lever, ed., Measure for Measure, Arden Shakespeare 2nd series (1965), introduction, pp. xxxiv-xlii, on the play's engagement with James I's ideas of governance and deputized authority.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 45

The Lever Arden 2nd series (1965) is a real edition with a xcviii-page introduction, placing pages xxxiv-xlii well within it; the introduction is known to cover James I's governance and deputized authority; the source is real and the claimed content is consistent with Lever's documented scholarly focus.
Both glosses ('remove' as departure; 'Mortality and mercy' as the sovereign's twin prerogatives of execution and pardon) are accurate and the formal-deputation reading is the consensus position.

anchor_text: some more test made of my metal, Before so noble and so great a figure Be stamped upon it
summary: Angelo puns on 'metal' and 'mettle' — two spellings often interchangeable in early modern English. 'Metal' (the material) leads directly into the coin-minting image: the Duke's authority is a great 'figure' (design on a coin) that will be 'stamped' on Angelo as deputy. 'Mettle' is the older spelling for courage, quality of character. Angelo asks to be tested before such high office is pressed on him.
detail: In Shakespeare's time 'metal' and 'mettle' were near-synonymous in spelling; the pun on the coin-making process (test the alloy before you mint it) was a familiar wit. 'Figure' could mean both a person of rank and the image on a coin; 'stamped' means both impressed (on coin-metal) and given official warrant. The Duke has just asked 'What figure of us think you he will bear?' (TLN 16) — Angelo here picks up that coin-imagery and turns it self-deprecatingly on himself. OED s.v. 'mettle / metal' notes the spellings were not consistently distinguished until the eighteenth century.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'mettle, metal' n.: 'mettle' was spelled 'metal' throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries; the two meanings (substance/quality of character) were deliberately exploited as a pun.

sources.citation: C. T. Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary, rev. R. D. Eagleson (1986), s.v. 'mettle' and 'metal.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 51

OED confirms 'mettle' was spelled 'metal' interchangeably through the seventeenth century and the dual meanings were exploited as a pun; Onions documents the same; both sources support the annotation.
The coin-minting pun is confirmed by the Duke's own 'figure' at TLN 16 and the text's explicit 'stamped upon it'; the metal/mettle spelling overlap is well-documented in OED.

anchor_text: leaven'd and prepared choice Proceeded to you
summary: 'Leaven'd' means slowly matured, fully thought through — the image is of dough that has had time to rise. Leaven (yeast) requires time to work; a 'leaven'd choice' is one that has fermented and developed over time, not a hasty decision. The Duke is telling Angelo the appointment was long deliberated, not impulsive.
detail: The bread-leavening metaphor for a decision given time to mature is unusual in Shakespeare and seems to have struck editors as striking. The Geneva Bible uses 'leaven' in Matthew 13:33 as a figure for something that works slowly and pervasively through a mass. The opposite of 'leaven'd' here would be a raw, undeveloped ('unleavened') choice. The word signals the Duke's care to present Angelo's elevation as premeditated, not circumstantial — important given the compressed departure that follows. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'leavened.'

anchor_text: I love the people, But do not like to stage me to their eyes: Though it do well, I do not relish well Their loud applause and 'aves' vehement
summary: 'Aves' (pronounced 'ah-vays') is the plural of the Latin ave — 'hail!' or 'God save!' — the crowd's shout of acclamation when a ruler appeared in public. The Duke confesses he dislikes public display and popularity-seeking, a passage that notoriously echoes James I's own professed distaste for crowds, published in his Basilikon Doron (1599) just before he became England's king in 1603.

anchor_text: sanctimonious pirate that went to sea with the ten commandments
summary: Lucio compares the First Gentleman to a pirate who took the Ten Commandments to sea but scratched out the one against stealing, since theft was his whole purpose. 'Sanctimonious' means making a show of holiness; the joke is that the pirate kept nine commandments while violating the very law that defined his trade.
detail: The Ten Commandments are the laws given by God to Moses on Sinai (Exodus 20:1-17, Geneva 1599). 'Thou shalt not steal' is the eighth commandment in Protestant numbering (Exodus 20:15). Lucio uses the story to expose the First Gentleman's own hypocrisy: he claims to want peace but is glad of a war that lets soldiers plunder. 'Razed' (TLN 99) means erased or scraped out — the pirate scraped that one commandment from his copy. 'Sanctimonious' carries the sense of false or performed piety, exactly the show of holiness the pirate keeps up while erasing the law that condemns his trade.

anchor_text: Grace is grace, despite of all controversy
summary: Lucio's quip pivots on 'grace' in two senses: divine grace (the theological gift of God's favour that can redeem sinners) and the grace said before meals. He has just mocked the Gentlemen for not knowing table-grace from any religion, and now spins the word into a mocking compliment ('you yourself art a wicked villain, despite of all grace') — meaning divine grace cannot redeem him.
detail: The wordplay is also a parody of a live Reformation controversy: whether saving 'grace' was given freely by God to the elect (Calvinist position) or co-operated with human merit (Catholic/Arminian position). Lucio ends the theological dispute by asserting 'Grace is grace, despite of all controversy' — a tautology that deflects the whole debate. The deflection is apt in a play obsessed with mercy versus law: whether divine grace intervenes where strict judgment would condemn is exactly the question Isabella poses to Angelo in 2.2. 'Despite of all controversy' parodies the earnest doctrinal disputations that divided English Protestants in the 1590s-1600s.

anchor_text: went but a pair of shears between us
summary: The First Gentleman means that he and Lucio are cut from the same cloth — the same kind of man. 'A pair of shears' is a tailor's scissors; the image is that both were shaped by the same bolt of fabric. Lucio twists it: they may come from the same cloth, but he is the fine 'velvet' and the Gentleman is the 'list' — the cheap selvage edge that trims the bolt.
detail: The exchange unfolds a sustained cloth-trade metaphor. A 'list' is the border or selvage of a woven cloth, the coarser strip cut away as waste. 'Velvet' is an expensive, pile-woven fabric; 'three-piled' velvet (TLN 119) has three rows of pile — the very richest grade. 'Kersey' (TLN 120) is a cheap, coarse woollen cloth. The Gentleman turns the velvet insult back: he would rather be plain English kersey than 'piled' — where 'piled' carries the bawdy sense of having the hair of a syphilitic patient fall out, so that 'French velvet' means venereal disease contracted from French prostitutes. 'French crown' (TLN 134) completes the joke: a French crown was a coin, but also the bald crown caused by syphilis ('the French disease').

The sustained cloth-trade metaphor (list/velvet/three-piled/kersey) is well-grounded; 'piled' as bald from mercury treatment for syphilis and 'French velvet' as venereal disease are standard readings in Onions and OED, and the forward link to 'French crown' at TLN 134 is textually sound.

anchor_text: Madam Mitigation comes
summary: Lucio greets Mistress Overdone with the ironic nickname 'Madam Mitigation' — a brothel-keeper is someone who 'mitigates,' or eases, the urgency of male desire. The name is a sardonic compliment, treating the bawd as a social service provider who softens the sharp edges of lust.
detail: The name belongs to a tradition of comic nicknaming: bawd-characters in Elizabethan drama often carry abstract nouns for names (Doll Tearsheet, Mistress Quickly). 'Mitigation' is a legal and theological term for the lessening of a penalty, which plants it in the play's vocabulary of law, guilt, and mercy from the first scene of the low plot. Lucio's vocabulary — 'purchased diseases,' 'French crown,' diseases as a kind of investment — treats the brothel entirely in commercial terms, the same frame Pompey uses when he argues that lechery is a legitimate trade.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary
sources.citation: Onions, C. T., A Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'mitigate': 'to lessen, moderate'; common in legal contexts.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 128

Reading 'Mitigation' as the easing or lessening of male urgency is the mainstream gloss; the secondary legal/theological resonance is defensible in a play saturated with those vocabularies, and the naming-tradition parallel (Doll Tearsheet, Mistress Quickly) is accurate.

anchor_text: A French crown more
summary: A 'French crown' was both a gold coin (worth about four shillings) and the baldness that syphilis — called 'the French disease' — caused by destroying hair at the crown of the head. Lucio is saying the First Gentleman has acquired more than money's worth of disease at the brothel, specifically the kind associated with French infection. The following lines on 'hollow bones' confirm the joke: bone-ache was a recognised symptom of late syphilis.
detail: Syphilis was called 'the French disease' or 'the French pox' in England (and 'the English disease' in France); both nations blamed each other for its spread, which began in Europe after 1493. 'Thy bones are hollow: impiety has made a feast of thee' (TLN 137-138) plays on the known symptom of syphilitic osteitis — hollowing and softening of the bones. Mercury, then used to treat syphilis, also caused hair loss, giving the 'French crown' bald-pate its second resonance. The sustained disease-banter of this scene is the play's first gloss on the law against fornication that Angelo is about to enforce.

The coin / syphilitic-bald-crown double meaning is entirely standard, and 'hollow bones' as syphilitic osteitis (confirmed by period medical knowledge and the continued disease-banter of the scene) is well-attested in OED and Schmidt.

anchor_text: he was ever precise in promise-keeping
summary: Lucio's word 'precise' is the standard Elizabethan label for a Puritan — a strict, scrupulously rule-following Protestant. Applied to Claudio keeping promises, it is a compliment, but the word choice already links this scene's world to Angelo, whom the Duke describes in the very next scene (1.3) as 'a man of a most precise stricture.' The two uses connect: Claudio's genuine conscientiousness ironically echoes the fake rectitude of the man who will condemn him.
detail: The term 'precisian' (one who is 'precise') was an Elizabethan byword for the strict, severe Puritan, used both as self-description by reformers and as mockery by their opponents. Angelo is the play's central 'precisian': a man whose cold public austerity conceals lawless private desire. Lucio's praise of Claudio for being 'precise in promise-keeping' is therefore doubly ironic — the quality Angelo lacks most is the honest integrity Claudio actually had. The verbal echo would register for an attentive audience.

'Precise' as Puritan/precisian is well-documented from the 1570s onward; the structural irony connecting Claudio's genuine conscientiousness to Angelo's false 'precise stricture' in 1.3 is a sound textual observation and not an over-reading.

anchor_text: the war, what with the sweat, what with the gallows, and what with poverty, I am custom-shrunk
summary: Mistress Overdone lists the four things that have cut her client base: war (soldiers dead or away), 'the sweat' (a sweating sickness epidemic), the gallows (executions, including now Claudio), and poverty. 'Custom-shrunk' means her trade has shrunk — she has fewer customers. The sweat epidemic is probably an outbreak of plague or sweating sickness; London suffered repeated disease epidemics in the early 1600s.
detail: The 'sweat' or 'sweating sickness' (sudor anglicus) was a distinctive and virulent English fever that swept the country in outbreaks of 1485, 1508, 1517, 1528, and 1551; by 1604 'the sweat' still meant epidemic disease. Alternatively, the play may refer to plague, which struck London hard in 1603 (the year James I came to the throne), killing thousands and closing the theatres. Either reading places the scene in a city under simultaneous pressure from official moral crackdown and epidemic — both cutting the brothel's trade. Mistress Overdone's speech is the play's clearest link between the fictional Vienna and the real London of c. 1603-04.

'Peculiar' means private or exclusive (a river not held in common, belonging to one owner). The metaphor figures Claudio as a poacher who has gone fishing in Juliet's 'river' without the legal right of marriage.

anchor_text: All houses in the suburbs of Vienna must be plucked down
summary: Angelo's proclamation orders the brothels of Vienna's suburbs demolished. 'Suburbs' is not incidental: in Shakespeare's London the area outside the City walls — Bankside in Southwark, the Liberty of Whitefriars — was where brothels, playhouses, and other unlicensed trades clustered, beyond the City's authority. 'Vienna' here is a thin cover for London, and the proclamation mirrors real Jacobean orders to pull down disorderly suburban houses.
detail: The 'stews' (brothels) of Bankside had existed since the Middle Ages; Henry VIII officially suppressed them in 1546, but they kept reopening in the liberties and suburbs. Early in James I's reign (1603-04), the Privy Council issued orders against disorderly suburban houses, and the plague of 1603 shut much of the city. Pompey's further distinction — the city houses 'shall stand for seed' because 'a wise burgher put in for them' — is a joke about civic corruption: the inner-city brothels survived because someone bribed the authorities. Shakespeare's Globe theatre stood on the Bankside — the same suburb the proclamation targets — which gives the scene an additional edge for its original audience.

anchor_text: rats that ravin down their proper bane
summary: 'Ravin' means to devour greedily, with an appetite that cannot check itself. 'Proper bane' means their own poison — the rat-poison that kills them. Claudio's image is of creatures so driven by thirst that they drink the very substance that will destroy them: his own 'liberty' (sexual freedom) has worked the same way.
detail: 'Ravin' (also 'raven,' verb) is a standard Elizabethan word for ravenous, predatory gorging; it survives in 'ravening.' 'Bane' in this period means both a cause of death and a specific poison (rat-bane = rat-poison). The simile economically captures the self-defeating logic of excess: the rats are destroyed by their own thirst, as Claudio's sexual appetite has led to his arrest. The OED records 'ravin' (v.) 'to devour voraciously' from the 14th century. Compare Macbeth's 'hath raven'd up / The drowsy syrups' and the 'ravin lion' in As You Like It.

anchor_text: Upon a true contract I got possession of Julietta's bed
summary: Claudio says he and Juliet are already bound by a 'true contract' — a valid private betrothal — but have not yet had the public ceremony ('denunciation of outward order') that would make the marriage visible to the world. In Elizabethan law a sworn de praesenti betrothal ('I take you as my wife, now') was nearly as binding as a church wedding; Claudio and Juliet were, by this standard, already married in all but a public announcement.
detail: Elizabethan canon law, inherited from the medieval church, distinguished two forms of betrothal: de praesenti ('I take you now') and de futuro ('I will take you'). A de praesenti contract was essentially a valid marriage; the couple could lawfully consummate it without a church ceremony, though the church strongly disapproved of doing so before the public rite. Claudio's defence is that their private vow makes the child legitimate under this logic — the same logic the Duke later uses to justify sending Mariana to Angelo's bed in the bed-trick. The hanging of Angelo's revived statute on Claudio is, on this reading, an injustice: Claudio was sinning against ceremony, not against the law of marriage itself. 'Denunciation' here means public declaration or proclamation (from Latin denuntiare, to announce formally).

anchor_text: fault and glimpse of newness
summary: Claudio is trying to figure out whether Angelo's harshness comes from a flaw ('fault') in the novelty of power, or from the man himself. 'Glimpse' here means a flash or sudden display — the brief dazzle of new authority. He is asking whether Angelo is cruel because he is new to power and overcompensating, or because cruelty is his nature.
detail: 'Glimpse' in this period could mean both a quick look and a sudden, brief manifestation of light — a flash rather than a sustained glow. The phrase 'fault and glimpse of newness' thus suggests that the excessive strictness might simply be the momentary flare-up of a new governor asserting himself. Claudio works through three alternative explanations (the novelty theory, the 'body politic' horse-and-rider theory, and the ambiguity of whether the tyranny is in the office or the man) before settling on the conclusion that Angelo acts 'for a name' — to make a reputation as a strict enforcer. All three possibilities keep open the question of Angelo's inner nature that the play will answer devastatingly.

anchor_text: enrolled penalties Which have, like unscour'd armour, hung by the wall
summary: 'Enrolled penalties' are penalties written into the statute rolls — laws on the books. Claudio's image is of armour left hanging on the wall so long it has gone rusty from disuse. Angelo has now reached down this forgotten statute against fornication and applied it, for the sake of making his name as a strict governor, to Claudio's case.
detail: 'Nineteen zodiacs' means nineteen years — one full circuit of the zodiac equals one year. The image of laws as disused armour underscores the arbitrariness of Claudio's predicament: the offence was always illegal, but the law had been a dead letter. Angelo's revival of it for purely reputational purposes ('for a name') is what Claudio finds unjust, not the law itself. The play thus opens a question about the difference between a law's existence and its selective enforcement — a question that scales up in the scenes that follow as Angelo proves to be personally guilty of exactly what he prosecutes.

anchor_text: my sister should the cloister enter, And there receive her approbation
summary: Isabella is about to enter the convent of the Order of Saint Clare as a novice, and is at the stage called 'approbation' — a probationary trial period in which the novice tests and is tested by the religious life before taking final vows. She has not yet committed herself irrevocably.
detail: The Order of Saint Clare (the Poor Clares), founded by Clare of Assisi in the 13th century, was among the strictest of female religious orders, requiring enclosure, poverty, and silence. 'Approbation' — Latin approbatio — was the formal period of probation before a novice's final profession of vows. The scene that follows (1.4 in many editions, but here the next scene) shows Isabella at the convent asking whether there might not be 'a more strict restraint' on the novices, which establishes her as genuinely drawn to the life rather than merely assigned to it. Her status as a novice rather than a fully professed nun is dramatically crucial: her vows are not yet absolute, and her chastity is not yet protected by the full weight of a vow sworn before God — though she will defend it as if it were.

anchor_text: prone and speechless dialect Such as moves men
summary: 'Prone' here does not mean lying face-down; it means inclined toward, apt, or ready — i.e. naturally disposed to persuasion. 'Speechless dialect' is the non-verbal communication of beauty, gesture, and bearing that can move a man without words. Claudio is telling Lucio that his sister's very presence, quite apart from what she says, will be persuasive.
detail: The Elizabethan sense of 'prone' as 'inclined, disposed, or tending toward' (OED sense 3) is now rare, surviving mainly in 'prone to error.' Claudio's formulation is deliberately paradoxical: a 'dialect' (a mode of speaking or communicating) that works without speech. He is arguing that Isabella's appearance as a beautiful, earnest young woman will work on Angelo's emotions even before she opens her mouth — an argument that proves accurately, catastrophically right, since it is exactly her chastity and eloquence combined that inflame Angelo's desire. The phrase anticipates the irony of what follows.

anchor_text: foolishly lost at a game of tick-tack
summary: Tick-tack was a real table game, a variant of backgammon (from the French tric-trac), in which players moved their men according to dice and scored by points and positions. The name carried an obvious sexual double sense, so that losing at 'tick-tack' means dying for the sake of sex. Lucio reduces Claudio's death sentence to a bad turn in a bawdy parlour game.
detail: The game is recorded from the sixteenth century; Florio's Worlde of Wordes (1598) glosses the Italian 'tric-trach' as 'ticke-tacke, a kind of play at tables.' The sexual resonance of the name was exploited by contemporary writers and is recorded in the slang record. Lucio's joke is characteristically callous: he has just offered to help save Claudio's life, but cannot resist reducing the whole situation to a dirty quip. The remark also marks Lucio's voice as the play's comic amoral chorus — the sort of man whose first response to his friend's mortal peril is a pun about sex.

anchor_text: dribbling dart of love Can pierce a complete bosom
summary: A 'dribbling dart' is a weak, glancing arrow that barely penetrates — the opposite of a clean, deep strike. Cupid's arrows conventionally pierce the heart; the Duke says his is a heart ('complete bosom') too fully armoured by seriousness for any such feeble shot to wound. He is emphatically denying that his reason for seeking the friar's company is a love affair.
detail: The adjective 'dribbling' carries a sense of weak, intermittent dripping, used here to belittle erotic love as a trivial, glancing force compared to the 'grave and wrinkled' purposes the Duke is about to describe. 'Complete bosom' means a fully resolved, self-contained heart — one without chink or gap for love to find. The image inverts the standard Petrarchan conceit of Cupid's arrow piercing an unguarded heart (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.468-474, in Golding's 1567 English translation). The Duke's rhetoric here is a pointed self-presentation: he wants Friar Thomas to understand from the outset that this visit is political, not amorous.

anchor_text: lov'd the life remov'd, And held in idle price to haunt assemblies
summary: 'The life remov'd' means a life withdrawn from public society — private, secluded, away from crowds. To hold something 'in idle price' is to value it cheaply, as something only the idle pursue. The Duke says he has always preferred withdrawal and thought little of attending crowded gatherings where wealth and youthful showing-off ('witless bravery') hold court.
detail: 'Removed' in Elizabethan usage means set apart, retired from the world — the sense still alive in 'a removed house' for an out-of-the-way dwelling. 'Idle price' is harder: 'idle' does not mean worthless but suggests frivolous, unproductive — the Duke 'prices' (values) haunting assemblies as a pursuit fit only for those with nothing serious to do. 'Witless bravery' means showy finery without understanding — 'bravery' in Elizabethan English regularly means fine clothes or ostentatious display, not courage (cf. Onions s.v. 'bravery'). The passage establishes the Duke's character as introspective and private — which makes his long absence from public governance both explained and questioned: he preferred study to rule.

anchor_text: A man of stricture and firm abstinence
summary: 'Stricture' means strict observance of rules — severity of practice. Angelo is introduced here as a man of iron self-discipline who neither bends the law nor gives way to appetite. The Duke is choosing him precisely because this rigid reputation makes Angelo the right instrument to enforce laws the Duke himself would find too harsh to apply. The play will test whether that strictness is genuine or a mask.
detail: 'Stricture' is rare: it appears only here in Shakespeare and means rigorous adherence, exactness of life — close to what contemporaries called being 'precise' or a 'precisian,' the nickname for stern Protestant reformers. 'Abstinence' reinforces the image of a man who has denied himself the ordinary pleasures of warmth, appetite, and sociability. Together the two words set up the play's central irony: the judge whose entire public identity is self-denial turns out to be the most dangerously covetous of all. The choice of Angelo thus exposes the Duke's own political calculation — he picks a man whose cold reputation will absorb the public's anger for enforcing unpopular laws while the Duke stays clean.

anchor_text: this fourteen years we have let sleep
summary: The Duke confesses that the laws against fornication have not been enforced for fourteen years under his watch, so that they are now 'dead to infliction' — meaningless threats. Angelo's sudden crackdown on Claudio is therefore not mere personal severity but the revival of laws the Duke himself allowed to go dormant. The Duke's guilt about his own permissiveness is his stated reason for using Angelo as a proxy enforcer.
detail: The admission is politically important and morally uncomfortable: the Duke acknowledges that the fault is his ('Sith 'twas my fault to give the people scope,' TLN 301). Having let the laws sleep so long, he judges it would be tyranny for him to enforce them in his own person — he would be punishing people for behaviour he effectively licensed. So he installs Angelo to do the enforcing while keeping his own hands clean. Critics debate whether this is prudent statecraft or cowardly evasion of responsibility. The Jacobean audience would recognize the situation: King James I's government issued repeated orders to suppress the brothels of the London suburbs at almost exactly the date of the play's first performance (c. 1603-04), making the dormant-law premise topical.

anchor_text: Lord Angelo is precise; Stands at a guard with envy
summary: 'Precise' was the standard contemporary word for a strict, self-righteous Protestant — what we might call a Puritan. Angelo 'stands at a guard with envy' means he is always on guard against desire or malice, as if braced with a sword. The Duke is describing a man whose entire identity is public virtue and denial — which the Duke now intends to test by leaving him in power.
detail: 'Precise' and 'precisian' were near-technical labels for the austere Protestant wing in Jacobean England — the men who wanted to close the theatres and the brothels and police private morality. Shakespeare uses the same type in Malvolio of Twelfth Night, called 'a kind of Puritan' (2.3). The phrase 'stands at a guard' is a fencing term: Angelo holds himself in a permanent defensive posture against any assault of appetite or ill-will ('envy' here meaning ill-feeling as well as covetousness). The closing lines of the scene — 'hence shall we see, / If power change purpose, what our seemers be' — signal that the Duke already suspects Angelo's precision may be performed rather than real, and plans to use the experiment to unmask it.

anchor_text: votarists of Saint Clare
summary: The Poor Clares are a Roman Catholic order of enclosed nuns founded by Saint Clare of Assisi in 1212, under the rule of Saint Francis. Their life was one of strict enclosure and poverty; novices like Isabella had not yet taken final vows. The scene dramatizes that enclosure directly: once professed, a nun could not speak to a man without the prioress present.
detail: The Order of Saint Clare (Ordo Sanctae Clarae) was known for the severity of its rule. Clare of Assisi (c. 1194-1253) founded it with Francis's help, and the 'Poor Clares' lived by strict poverty, enclosure, and a regimen of fasting and prayer. Isabella's desire for 'a more strict restraint' signals her rigorist temperament, which will later collide head-on with Angelo's equally rigid legalism. That the woman most resistant to moral compromise is herself drawn to the most austere of women's orders is one of the play's taut structural ironies.

anchor_text: you are yet unsworn
summary: Francisca explains that Isabella, as a novice who has not yet taken final vows, may still speak freely with men. Once professed (having 'vow'd'), the rule requires a nun to have the prioress present for any conversation with a man, and she must either speak without showing her face, or show her face without speaking. The double prohibition encodes the strict Clarian enclosure rule.
detail: The twin prohibition ('you must not show your face' / 'you must not speak') reflects the constitutions of the enclosed contemplative orders. A novice occupied a probationary liminal position: she lived inside the community but retained the legal capacity of a layperson and had not yet surrendered all civil rights. The audience would notice that Francisca, fully professed, retreats when she hears the male voice, leaving the as-yet-unbound Isabella to handle Lucio. The scene sets up Isabella's transitional status as something Lucio will later exploit: she can still go into the world to plead for her brother.

anchor_text: those cheek-roses / Proclaim you are no less
summary: Lucio greets Isabella 'Hail, virgin, if you be' and answers his own question by pointing to her rosy cheeks as proof. The conditional greeting ('if you be') is mildly impudent: a well-born woman's virginity was assumed, not openly doubted. Lucio's first words thus establish his mode: frank, testing, bawdy at the edges.
detail: 'If you be' is a mock-qualification that implies a man of Lucio's world cannot simply assume chastity. The phrasing glances at the ribald sense: 'cheek-roses' as a sign of sexual innocence or, equally, as a blush of awareness. Lucio immediately converts his flippancy into extravagant compliment ('ensky'd and sainted,' line 356), but the opening gambit sets him as someone who measures innocence from outside it. anchor_text: seem the lapwing, and to jest, / Tongue far from heart
summary: The lapwing (peewit) was proverbially associated with deceit because it calls loudly and flutters away from its nest to mislead predators away from its chicks. 'To seem the lapwing' means to perform one thing while meaning another — in Lucio's case, to flirt and jest with women while the words mean nothing. He is confessing his own usual dishonesty in order to swear he will be straight with Isabella.

anchor_text: ensky'd and sainted; / By your renouncement an immortal spirit
summary: 'Ensky'd' means placed among the heavenly bodies, lifted into the sky, made celestial. Lucio says that by taking religious vows ('your renouncement' of the world) Isabella has become, in his eyes, not a mortal woman at all but an immortal spirit among the saints. The word appears only here in Shakespeare's works and is probably his coinage.
detail: 'Renouncement' refers to the renunciation of the world required by the monastic vow: the candidate formally renounces property, autonomy, and sexuality. Lucio's extravagant compliment recodes Isabella's vow-taking as a kind of ascension — she has, in effect, died to the world and become angelic. His language here ('ensky'd,' 'immortal spirit,' 'saint') echoes the discourse of beatification and intercession, the Catholic sense in which a saint could be prayed to as a powerful heavenly mediator. This also sets up the satire on Isabella's position: she can intercede for sinners before God, but can she intercede for one particular sinner before Angelo?

anchor_text: from the seedness the bare fallow brings / To teeming foison; even so her plenteous womb / Expresseth his full tilth and husbandry
summary: Lucio describes Claudio and Juliet's pregnancy through agricultural metaphor: 'seedness' is sowing, 'bare fallow' is unploughed ground, 'teeming foison' is plentiful harvest, 'tilth' is cultivated farmland, and 'husbandry' means both the practice of farming and the role of a husband. Her pregnant body is the field; his sexual act is the tillage. The pun on 'husbandry' (farming / being a husband) carries the irony: Claudio has done the work of a husband without being one.
detail: Agricultural metaphors for sexuality were commonplace in Elizabethan English; 'field / tilling' for the woman's body, 'ploughing / sowing' for the sexual act, and 'harvest / fruit' for pregnancy formed a stable repertoire. 'Foison' (from Old French, via Latin fusio) means an abundant yield. 'Tilth' (from Old English) is the primary sense of cultivated land but, in context, the sexual labour that produced the pregnancy. The passage makes a philosophical point through the metaphor: the progression from bare ground to harvest is natural, inevitable, and good; the human law that punishes Claudio has interrupted a natural process mid-course. Lucio's imagery implicitly frames Angelo's statute as a crime against nature.

anchor_text: a man whose blood / Is very snow-broth; one who never feels / The wanton stings and motions of the sense
summary: Lucio's image of Angelo as a man whose blood is 'snow-broth' — icy, thin, almost frozen water — is the defining characterization of the play's 'precise' Puritan type. Blood in Elizabethan physiology carried the passions and desires; cold, thin blood meant the absence of warmth, appetite, and human feeling. The word 'precise' in this and the surrounding passages (compare 1.3: 'a man of a most precise stricture') was the standard Jacobean label for a severe, self-righteous Puritan.
detail: Elizabethan humoral physiology held that the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) governed temperament. Hot blood meant passion and vitality; cold, phlegmatic blood meant sluggishness or inhuman restraint. 'Stings and motions of the sense' (line 383) means the sexual urges and impulses of the body. Angelo's self-suppression of appetite through 'profits of the mind, study, and fast' (line 385) characterizes the Puritan reformer who disciplines the body by disciplining the flesh — a figure the Jacobean theatre regularly satirized. The dramatic irony is structural: the audience already knows from 1.3 that Angelo will be placed in charge of Vienna's moral crackdown, and they are being primed to watch his icy self-control melt.

sources.name: Elizabethan-Jacobean usage
sources.citation: 'Precise' and 'precisian': common Elizabethan-Jacobean terms for the strict, austere Puritan. Angelo is introduced at 1.3 as 'a man of a most precise stricture'; compare the stage-Puritan Malvolio in Twelfth Night, 'a kind of Puritan' (2.3). Cf. OED s.v. 'precise' sense 3a: rigidly observant of rule.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 381

The humoral reading and 'precise/precisian' gloss are sound, but identifying Angelo as a stage-Puritan type is contested scholarship (the play does not label him Puritan outright), and importing Malvolio as a parallel risks conflating distinct dramatic contexts.

anchor_text: Which have for long run by the hideous law, / As mice by lions
summary: Lucio says Vienna's fornication law has long been ignored — people scurried past it the way mice scurry past a sleeping lion. The simile captures the paradox: the law existed and was technically in force, but no one enforced it. Angelo's innovation is not to write a new law but to wake the old one.
detail: The 'lion' is the statute itself, so deadly that it has been given a wide berth by instinct, but never provoked. This is a pointed comment on the Duke's years of lax governance: the 'hideous law' was on the books but functionally dead, its terror purely theoretical. Angelo's cruelty (in Lucio's framing) is not that he invents a punishment but that he decides to apply what the law already says. This is the play's first direct characterization of the political situation Isabella is walking into: she will need to argue against the letter of a law that no one disputes, applying mercy as a higher principle than statutory enforcement.

The simile is accurately glossed — the dormant law awakened by Angelo, not a new law — and the political framing of the Duke's lax governance is directly supported by the surrounding text and by 1.3.

anchor_text: Our doubts are traitors, / And make us lose the good we oft might win / By fearing to attempt
summary: Lucio coins a sharp sententious maxim: self-doubt ('doubts') are called traitors because they betray us by preventing action, causing us to lose achievable goods through fear of trying. The metaphor gives an abstract psychological state — hesitation — a political charge: the doubter is their own enemy, a fifth columnist within the self. The lines are among the play's most-quoted.
detail: The rhetorical figure is sententia — a brief, pointed, universal moral observation — a standard oratorical device taught in the Elizabethan grammar school and valued in both oratory and drama as a marker of wit and eloquence. Ironically, these words are spoken by Lucio, the play's self-proclaimed libertine and liar, coaching the virtuous Isabella to assert herself. The scene repeatedly stages this incongruity: the morally unreliable Lucio correctly reads the situation and gives Isabella sound strategic advice. The sentiment is close to Seneca's 'qui nusquam est, nusquam potest esse' — but Shakespeare's form is pithier and the context more dramatic.

anchor_text: make a scarecrow of the law
summary: Angelo uses a scarecrow as a figure for a law that stands idle without enforcing fear: a fake that frightens at first, then becomes a roost ('their perch, and not their terror'). He is arguing that unused laws invite contempt, just as birds that get used to a scarecrow ignore it.
detail: The argument opens the play's central legal debate: should law be enforced strictly, reviving statutes long dormant, or moderately? Angelo stands for strict enforcement; Escalus will urge mercy. The scarecrow image is vivid and proverbially familiar: if the law stands in the field and does nothing, lawbreakers eventually settle on it. The metaphor also quietly incriminates Angelo — he is himself a kind of scarecrow of virtue, a terrifying outward form whose inside is hollow.

anchor_text: keen, and rather cut a little Than fall and bruise to death
summary: Escalus counters Angelo's hard line with a surgical image: a sharp, careful cut (a lesser punishment) is better than a blunt fall that bruises and kills. He is arguing for mercy toward Claudio rather than execution, using the image of a surgeon who makes a precise incision rather than a brutal blow.

His argument is that measured mercy preserves the body politic; Angelo's absolute enforcement, by contrast, is a blunt instrument that could destroy more than it cures. 'Fall' here has the sense of the weight of the law descending without discernment.

summary: 'Strait' here means 'strict' or 'narrow' in moral conduct, not the modern spelling 'straight' (meaning direct or honest). Escalus is acknowledging Angelo's famously tight, uncompromising virtue. The word carries no geographic sense here; it belongs to the same family as 'straitlaced.'

anchor_text: 'Tis one thing to be tempted, Escalus, Another thing to fall
summary: Angelo distinguishes between feeling temptation and actually giving in to it. The language echoes standard Protestant theology: temptation itself is not sin, only the yielding is. The audience, who knows Angelo will shortly yield to his own temptation for Isabella, hears the irony at once.

Shakespeare has Angelo speak correct theology and then proceed to illustrate the very failure he here condemns. The line is the play's first and sharpest dramatic irony: Angelo is at this moment being tempted and will fall.

anchor_text: jury, passing on the prisoner's life, May, in the sworn twelve, have a thief or two
summary: Angelo argues that a jury of twelve judging a prisoner's life might itself include a guilty man among its number — yet the law works with what is public and proven, not with hidden guilt. 'Passing on' means giving a verdict on. This is standard Elizabethan trial procedure: twelve sworn jurors decided capital cases.
detail: Juries of twelve men for felony trials were the Elizabethan common-law standard. Angelo's argument is a logical one: hidden guilt does not disqualify a juror, because the law can only act on what it knows. The point quietly prefigures his own situation — he is condemning Claudio for a private sin while harbouring a worse one himself. 'What's open made to justice, / That justice seizes': justice is reactive, not omniscient.

The gloss on 'passing on' as delivering a verdict and the note on twelve-man felony juries are accurate; the annotation reads the text and its legal context correctly, and the prefigurative note on Angelo is defensible.

anchor_text: 'Tis very pregnant
summary: 'Pregnant' here means 'obvious' or 'clear-cut' — full of meaning, as a swollen case is full. Angelo is saying: 'this is perfectly evident.' The modern sense of 'with child' was common too, but here the word means 'convincingly full' or 'manifestly plain.'

'Pregnant' meaning 'obvious, clear, convincing' is well-attested in Onions and OED for Elizabethan usage; the gloss is accurate and the parenthetical on the modern sense is a helpful caveat, not an overreach.

anchor_text: Bring him his confessor; let him be prepard
summary: Angelo orders that a priest be brought to hear Claudio's confession before execution — a standard practice in Catholic and early Protestant England, ensuring the condemned died spiritually prepared. The confessor (a 'shrift-father') would hear the prisoner's sins, grant absolution, and administer last rites.
detail: The practice of hearing a prisoner's confession on the morning of execution was routine in pre-Reformation England and persisted in modified form afterward. The disguised Duke later takes over this priestly function himself, hearing confessions and preparing the condemned — which is part of what makes his friar-disguise so useful dramatically and so ethically complex. The 'confessor' here is a real clergyman; later the 'confessor' is the Duke himself.

Bringing a confessor before execution is accurately described as standard practice, and the note that the Duke later takes over this function is a genuine thematic point, not over-interpretation.

anchor_text: that's the utmost of his pilgrimage
summary: Angelo means this is the furthest point Claudio's life will reach — tomorrow morning's execution is the end of his journey. 'Pilgrimage' was a common metaphor for a human life: the soul journeys from birth to death as a pilgrim. 'Utmost' means 'farthest' or 'outermost limit.'

anchor_text: Some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall: Some run from brakes of vice
summary: Escalus speaks in couplets — a signal that these lines carry sententious, proverbial weight. The couplet is a small epigram: the world is upside down, wickedness advances some while virtue ruins others, and the law punishes only those it catches. 'Brakes of vice' means thickets (brake = a dense undergrowth) of sinful conduct — people crash through them without penalty.

The paradox — that sin may be the more successful strategy — indicts the system Angelo is enforcing. The couplet also echoes the Sermon on the Mount's observation that the rain falls on the just and unjust alike (Matthew 5:45).

summary: Elbow means 'who commit their offences in brothels' — 'common houses' is Elizabethan legal and colloquial shorthand for brothels, houses of ill repute open to the public ('common' as in 'commonly available'). He characteristically mangles his meaning: he intends to condemn them, but his phrasing almost sounds like a legal definition.

anchor_text: two notorious benefactors
summary: Elbow means 'malefactors' (wrongdoers) but says 'benefactors' (well-doers, patrons). This is his first malapropism — the comic substitution of a word for its near-opposite — and Angelo immediately corrects it: 'Benefactors! Well; what benefactors are they? are they not malefactors?' Elbow's blundering anti-language defines his character throughout the scene.
detail: A malapropism is the substitution of a similar-sounding wrong word for the right one, usually with opposite meaning. Elbow's 'benefactors / malefactors' pattern runs throughout this scene: he later says 'detest' for 'protest,' 'cardinally' for 'carnally,' 'respected' for 'suspected,' and 'honourable man' to address the prisoner Pompey. The device was made famous in the novel by Mrs Malaprop in Sheridan's The Rivals (1775), but the device is older; Elbow prefigures Dogberry in Much Ado. Escalus's aside, 'Do you hear how he misplaces?' (TLN 502), gives it its critical label.

anchor_text: vice that most I do abhor, And most desire should meet the blow
summary: Isabella opens her plea with a confession that makes her task harder: she abhors the offence Claudio committed (fornication) and wants it punished — yet she must argue for mercy toward the person who committed it. anchor_text: No ceremony that to great ones 'longs, Not the king's crown nor the deputed sword

anchor_text: all the souls that were were forfeit once; And He that might the vantage best have took
summary: Isabella invokes the Christian doctrine of original sin: all human souls were once guilty (forfeit) before God because of the Fall, and God — who had the best advantage of any creditor — did not exact the full penalty but instead found a remedy: the redemption of mankind through Christ. anchor_text: He's not prepared for death. Even for our kitchens We kill the fowl of season
summary: Isabella argues that even for cooking we choose birds that are properly seasoned (at the right time, in good condition); executing Claudio now, spiritually unprepared to die, shows less care for God than we give our dinner. 'Fowl of season' means birds taken in their proper season, when they are fit. The comparison of the condemned man to table-fowl is deliberately homely and disarming.

The kitchen analogy grounds the theological point in daily experience, making the irony vivid — we treat poultry with more ceremony than Angelo is giving a human soul.

anchor_text: The law hath not been dead, though it hath slept
summary: Angelo defends reviving a dormant law: the statute against fornication was always on the books; it simply had not been enforced. Angelo's 'like a prophet / Looks in a glass that shows what future evils' figures the law as a mirror or prophetic glass showing the shape of wickedness to come — a visual conceit that gives the law an almost supernatural foresight.

anchor_text: it is excellent To have a giant's strength; but it is tyrannous To use it like a giant
summary: Isabella turns to a direct attack on the abuse of power: strength is fine to possess, but using it like a giant is tyranny. In classical and biblical tradition, giants were the byword for brute, ungoverned force — strength without wisdom or mercy. The paradox is that the same quality (great strength/authority) is admirable or monstrous depending entirely on how it is used.

The image sets up Isabella's more elaborate Jove comparison that follows immediately: if even the king of the gods restrains his thunderbolt, a petty officer should restrain his authority still more. The aphorism became one of the most quoted lines in the play.

anchor_text: Could great men thunder As Jove himself does, Jove would ne'er be quiet
summary: Jove (Jupiter) was the Roman king of the gods whose weapon was the thunderbolt. Isabella argues that if powerful men could hurl thunder like Jove, they would never stop — every minor official would blast away. The point is that Jove himself uses the thunderbolt sparingly, which is what makes him majestic rather than merely noisy.

Ovid's Metamorphoses Book 1 (the council of the gods, and Jove's decision on punishment versus reformation of mankind) is the direct background. The irony Isabella is building: Jove, the ultimate authority, restrains his most terrible weapon; Angelo, a petty deputy, exercises his power at full force. The contrast between the god's restraint and the petty officer's noisy overreach is central to her whole argument about mercy and authority.

anchor_text: Dress'd in a little brief authority,-- Most ignorant of what he's most assured, His glassy essence
summary: Isabella describes the arrogant official: dressed in the costume of authority for a brief time, most ignorant precisely about the thing he thinks he is most certain of — his own soul or nature ('glassy essence'). 'Glassy essence' is one of the play's most debated phrases: it likely means the fragile, transparent, or mirror-like soul — the inner self that reflects the divine image but is also brittle and easily broken.
detail: 'Glassy' combines at least two senses: transparent (revealing) and fragile (breakable). The 'essence' is the soul understood philosophically as the true inner nature of a person, created in God's image. The irony is that the man most certain of his own virtue (Angelo) is least able to see himself clearly — his glass is opaque to him even as he turns it on others. The passage has been related by editors to Platonic and Neoplatonic discussions of the soul as a mirror of the divine; others read 'glassy' as simply 'fragile.'

summary: The ape was a Renaissance symbol of imitation without understanding — an animal that mimics human actions absurdly. anchor_text: Hath yet a kind of medicine in itself That skins the vice o' the top. Go to your bosom; Knock there

anchor_text: Not with fond shekels of the tested gold, Or stones, whose rates are either rich or poor

'That way going' admits the direction without yet naming the destination. 'Prayers cross' carries a secondary sense: her prayers and his desires meet head-on, cancel each other out. anchor_text: lying by the violet, in the sun Do, as the carrion does, not as the flower, Corrupt with virtuous season
summary: Angelo compares himself to a piece of rotting flesh ('carrion') lying beside a violet in the sun: the sun that makes the flower bloom makes the carrion rot faster. The same 'virtuous season' (good weather, pure circumstances — Isabella's virtue) has the opposite effect on him: it corrupts him rather than inspiring him. This is his shocked self-diagnosis of how perverse his desire is.
detail: The image is a formal paradox: the same cause (warm sun, virtue) produces opposite effects in different natures. The violet is specifically chosen — it is the flower most associated with modesty and virtue in early modern symbolism. 'Carrion' as dead flesh being corrupted by the very warmth that nourishes the living is vivid and self-disgusting: Angelo knows he is responding to Isabella's goodness as base matter responds to warmth, not as a living soul should. This extends naturally into his next question — 'Can it be / That modesty may more betray our sense / Than woman's lightness?' — i.e. can purity be more sexually provocative than overt promiscuity?

anchor_text: Shall we desire to raze the sanctuary, And pitch our evils there
summary: Angelo likens Isabella's chastity to a sacred sanctuary: his own desire is the wicked impulse to demolish the holy place and plant ('pitch') his sins there. To violate a sanctuary was sacrilege and a crime in both civil and church law. The image makes his lust for Isabella explicit to himself and to the audience for the first time.
detail: 'Sanctuary' held a precise legal meaning in early modern England: a church or consecrated place where a fugitive could claim protection from arrest. To 'raze' it means to tear it flat. The image of profaning holy ground to 'pitch' one's evils there (set up one's wickedness, like pitching a tent) makes Angelo's self-awareness luridly architectural: he is designing the desecration even as he names it. 'Pitch' carried a secondary sense of something black and defiling (pitch as tar). The frank sexual import — 'Having waste ground enough, / Shall we desire to raze the sanctuary' — reads Isabella's body as a consecrated space Angelo means to violate.

anchor_text: Thieves for their robbery have authority When judges steal themselves
summary: Angelo reasons to himself that if judges commit the same crimes they punish in others, they give thieves a justification for their own robberies — the law loses all its authority. The logic is a self-accusation: if he, who condemned Claudio for fornication, now desires the same thing, he has forfeited his right to judge. This is the most explicit statement of the play's central moral problem.
detail: The aphorism crystallizes the theme that will occupy the rest of the play: the gap between the judge's public role and private conduct. It also foreshadows the later plot, in which Angelo does commit precisely the vice he is punishing — and the play tests whether the Duke's pardon (or the forced marriage to Mariana) can resolve the resulting contradiction. The argument anticipates Isabella's 2.2 plea and Matthew 7:1-5 (the beam and the mote): judge not, lest you be judged by the same standard.

anchor_text: impression of keen whips I'd wear as rubies, And strip myself to death, as to a bed
summary: Isabella says she would endure flogging willingly ('wear as rubies') and walk naked to her own execution ('strip myself to death') as if going joyfully to bed — rather than yield her chastity. The imagery draws on the language of Christian martyrdom: early saints were depicted wearing their wounds as crowns and jewels, counting suffering in the body as glory.

Their wounds were routinely figured in hagiography as adornments, even as bridal preparations. Isabella, a novice of the Franciscan Order of Saint Clare (one of the strictest female orders), would know this tradition well. The 'bed' image is deliberately ambiguous: it sounds almost like erotic language, but refers to the bed of death and the marriage bed of martyrdom — joining Christ — that virginal saints were promised. The passage is Isabella at her most extreme, and has divided critics between admiration for her integrity and discomfort at its cost to Claudio.

anchor_text: Better it were a brother died at once Than that a sister, by redeeming him, Should die for ever
summary: Isabella says it is literally better for Claudio to die ('at once' — bodily, in time) than for her to yield her chastity and thereby 'die for ever' — meaning lose her soul eternally. She is measuring a temporal death against spiritual damnation, and choosing the temporal for her brother rather than the eternal for herself.

Isabella's logic is theologically consistent: if she commits a mortal sin to save Claudio's body, she trades her soul's eternal life for his temporal one — a bad bargain. The phrasing also anticipates the play's central irony: Angelo actually intends to execute Claudio anyway, so the 'exchange' is doubly worthless. The line has been read as Isabella's finest moment and as her coldest — the question being whether her certainty about Claudio's willingness to die for her honour is admirable or presumptuous.

anchor_text: If not a feodary, but only he, Owe, and succeed by weakness
summary: A 'feodary' (also spelled 'fedary') is a feudal tenant — a person who holds land in exchange for service to a lord, and who therefore shares the lord's fortunes. Isabella is saying: if Claudio were the only person, not a sharer in general human weakness, who is guilty of and must answer for ('owe and succeed by') frailty, then let him die. But since frailty is universal ('we are all frail'), singling him out for death is unjust.
detail: The legal-feudal term 'feodary' (from Latin feodarius, a holder of a fief) is used here in its figurative sense of 'partner, sharer in common obligations.' 'Owe and succeed by weakness' = is bound and inherits by the fault of frailty. Isabella's argument is a direct counter to Angelo's 'We are all frail' (TLN 1069): she takes the concession and uses it against him — if all humans are co-tenants of frailty, you cannot execute just one for the common condition. Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'feodary' (a vassal or confederate).

anchor_text: as the glasses where they view themselves; Which are as easy broke as they make forms. Women! Help heaven! men their creation mar In profiting by them
summary: Isabella seizes Angelo's 'women are frail' and turns it into a bitter accusation. Women are 'frail' like mirrors (easily broken, and easy to make reflections in — i.e. easy to imprint); but it is men who corrupt ('mar') the creation of women by exploiting that frailty for their own gain. 'Soft as our complexions are, / And credulous to false prints' means vulnerable to being stamped with false impressions, as wax takes a seal.
detail: The glass/mirror conceit runs through two punning senses of 'form': (1) reflections or images (a mirror makes visual forms); (2) to seduce, to 'form' a woman's behaviour. 'Easy broke as they make forms' = as easy to shatter as they are to imprint. 'Complexions' carries both the usual sense (skin colour, beauty) and the humoral sense (the mix of qualities in a person's temperament). 'Credulous to false prints' reaches for the wax-seal image already used in the coinage speech: women are soft enough to take false impressions stamped on them by men. Isabella's outburst is rhetorical self-deprecation that is simultaneously an accusation: she is out-arguing Angelo by agreeing with him while turning the charge back on its source.

anchor_text: if you be one,--as you are well express'd By all external warrants,--show it now By putting on the destin'd livery
summary: Angelo tells Isabella to 'show' she is a woman by 'putting on the destin'd livery' — i.e. by performing the role of compliance ('livery' is a servant's uniform, the dress of one's master's household) that her destiny as a woman supposedly requires. The phrase twists the vocabulary of feudal service into an argument for sexual submission: being a woman means wearing the 'uniform' of yielding to men.
detail: 'Livery' in the Elizabethan period had a rich range of legal and social meanings: the household uniform worn by servants of a lord; the legal delivery of property to an heir; the colours or badge of a patron. Angelo's use of 'destin'd livery' is coercive in two registers at once: it invokes the feudal/social obligation of a dependent (woman's subordinate place in the hierarchy) and it implies a natural, predestined suit of clothing that a woman must eventually put on. Isabella's response — 'I have no tongue but one: gentle, my lord, / Let me intreat you, speak the former language' (TLN 1089-90) — is a refusal to accept his redefinition of her identity.

anchor_text: little honour to be much believed, And most pernicious purpose!--Seeming, seeming!
summary: Isabella's repeated 'Seeming, seeming!' is a two-word summary of the play's central moral problem: Angelo's entire public persona is false appearance. 'Seeming' (from Anglo-French sembler, to appear) means the gap between outward show and inner reality. Her cry collapses the whole scene into one word and names the theme of the play — appearance, hypocrisy, the judge who is not what he seems.
detail: The word 'seeming' and its cognates ('seem,' 'seemed,' 'seeming') are among the most loaded words in Shakespeare's problem plays and tragedies: Hamlet rails at 'seeming' (1.2); Iago promises he is 'not what I am' (Othello 1.1). In Measure for Measure it has appeared in Angelo's own mouth at TLN 955 ('false seeming') and recurs here as Isabella's verdict on him. The rhetorical figure is epanalepsis (repetition of a word for emphasis). Her outburst also marks the transition of the scene: she stops trying to reinterpret Angelo's hints charitably and names what he is doing.

Identifying 'Seeming, seeming!' as epanalepsis naming the play's central theme (appearance vs. reality) is sound; the cross-references to Hamlet and Iago are illustrative rather than over-claimed, and the annotation correctly notes this marks a pivot point in the scene where Isabella abandons charitable misreading of Angelo.

anchor_text: I give my sensual race the rein: Fit thy consent to my sharp appetite
summary: 'Race' here means headlong rushing or rush of passion (not a competition), and 'give the rein' means to let the horse run unchecked. Angelo says he is letting his sexual desire bolt like an uncontrolled horse. The equestrian metaphor for unleashed lust — giving the 'rein' to passion — was a standard figure for abandoning self-governance.
detail: The horse-and-rider image for reason governing passion was a classical and Renaissance commonplace derived from Plato's Phaedrus (the charioteer and two horses of the soul) and from Cicero and Seneca on self-mastery. Here Angelo reverses the expected moral: instead of the virtuous rider reining in the horse, he deliberately drops the reins and lets appetite run. 'Race' in the sense of 'swift course' or 'impetuous movement' is documented in OED s.v. 'race,' n.2, sense 6. The image of a runaway horse for lust or passionate excess appears across Shakespeare (cf. 2 Henry IV 4.4 on the body's 'race of youth').

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1112

'Race' in the sense of a swift headlong course (OED n.2 sense 6) and the horse-and-rider moral metaphor (reason as rider, passion as horse) are both correct and well-attested early modern commonplaces; the annotation stops short of over-reading by not over-insisting on the Platonic charioteer specifically.

anchor_text: Lay by all nicety and prolixious blushes That banish what they sue for
summary: 'Nicety' means fastidious reserve or over-refinement of virtue; 'prolixious' (a Shakespearean coinage) means long-winded or drawn-out — here applied to the extended blushes of affected modesty. Angelo is telling Isabella to drop the 'teasing' performance of reluctance that, he claims, is really just advertising what she wants: the blushes 'banish what they sue for,' i.e. they drive away the very thing they secretly petition for.
detail: 'Nicety' from Latin nescire is used by Shakespeare and contemporaries for excessive scrupulousness, over-delicate prudishness; OED s.v. 'nicety,' n., sense 2 (precision or delicacy amounting to affectation). 'Prolixious' (TLN 1114) is Shakespeare's only use of the word in the canon — a nonce-formation from 'prolix' (long-winded) applied to a blush that drags on. Both words belong to Angelo's strategy of reframing Isabella's genuine refusal as a form of coy enticement — a rhetorical manoeuvre that attempts to deprive her 'no' of its honest meaning. The phrase has been used by later critics to analyse the victim-blaming logic of sexual coercion.

'Nicety' as fastidious or prudish reserve and 'prolixious' as a Shakespearean nonce-formation from 'prolix' are correctly glossed; the annotation accurately identifies Angelo's move as reframing genuine refusal as coy enticement, which is what the text literally says ('That banish what they sue for').

anchor_text: Isabel, live chaste, and, brother, die: More than our brother is our chastity
summary: In her final couplet Isabella resolves to let Claudio die rather than yield her body to Angelo. 'More than our brother is our chastity' states the play's hardest moral equation: for Isabella, chastity — her spiritual identity, her vows to the Order of Saint Clare, and her soul's salvation — outweighs even brotherly love. The line has been both the play's most admired and most contested.
detail: The line is the sharpest expression of the Renaissance doctrine that a woman's chastity is her defining honour and the condition of her spiritual life. Conduct literature (Vives, Juan Luis; The Instruction of a Christian Woman, 1523) and the theology of holy orders would both support Isabella's reasoning: she is a novice in one of the most strictly enclosed religious orders; her chastity is not a personal preference but a sacred vow. The tension is that Claudio is innocent of any harm to her, and his death is the price. Modern productions often stage the line as Isabella's most painful moment rather than her most confident. See the reference cards for chastity-and-the-double-standard and the-bed-trick, which is the device the Duke will use precisely to resolve this dilemma without Isabella having to make good on her resolve.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1136

The reading of Isabella's final couplet as an expression of Renaissance chastity doctrine in the context of holy orders is sound and well-grounded; the Vives citation is appropriate for the conduct-literature background, and the annotation acknowledges the critical controversy around the line rather than resolving it artificially.

anchor_text: Be absolute for death
summary: 'Absolute' here means fully resolved, unconditionally decided. The disguised Duke, acting as a friar-confessor, counsels Claudio to make his peace with death entirely, without holding any back-door hope of life. The stance is a Stoic ideal: freedom comes from surrendering the thing you fear losing.
detail: The Duke's consolation speech (TLN 1144-1180) is one of Shakespeare's most concentrated pieces of Stoic argument, drawing on commonplaces from Seneca and Cicero: life is a loan, not a possession; the body is subject to ailment, age, and fortune; the self is not a fixed thing; and death levels all distinctions. The speech has been debated as a sincere philosophical preparation or as cynical manipulation from a Duke who knows Claudio may yet be reprieved. The word 'absolute' carries its Latin sense of absolved or freed (absolutus) as well as simply 'complete.'

'Absolute' as 'unconditionally resolved' is well-attested in Schmidt and Onions, and the secondary Latin etymology (absolutus = freed) is a defensible enrichment of the Stoic argument, not an overreach.

anchor_text: Servile to all the skiey influences
summary: 'Skiey influences' are the effects of the stars and planets on human bodies and temperaments. Elizabethans widely believed that celestial bodies influenced health, mood, and fate — astrology was not fringe belief but the received science of the heavens. The Duke is arguing that the body is merely a puppet of the sky's movements, which is no great thing to cling to.

anchor_text: thou art death's fool; For him thou labour'st by thy flight to shun
summary: The 'fool' of a lord was his jester, kept in service — but 'death's fool' reverses the usual power: life runs away from death, which only makes death laugh, because fleeing is pointless. Every attempt to escape death brings you no closer to safety; the fool capers for his master's amusement without realising it.
detail: The image draws on the medieval tradition of the Danse Macabre, in which Death leads all ranks of humanity — emperor, pope, peasant — in a dance to their graves. The 'fool' of a great lord was the one performer who could mock everyone, including his master, but was still owned by him. Here life becomes the fool and Death the lord: however much life rants and capers to avoid its master, it still serves him. The argument is Stoic: the only freedom from the fear of death is to stop treating death as something to outrun.

anchor_text: thy complexion shifts to strange effects, After the moon
summary: 'Complexion' meant not just skin tone but one's overall temperament and bodily constitution, made up of the four humours. The moon was believed to govern moisture in the body and so to make temperament changeable and unstable — lunacy (luna = moon) was the extreme form of this lunar influence. The Duke is arguing that since you have no fixed, moon-independent self, life is not worth clinging to.
detail: Galenic medicine held that the four humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) governed temperament, and that the moon — the nearest celestial body — controlled moisture and so shifted the balance of humours through its phases. 'Complexion' (from Latin complexio, 'combination') referred to the particular blend of humours that made each person's characteristic nature; to say it 'shifts after the moon' is to deny that character is stable or truly one's own. The broader argument links to the instability of the 'body' annotated above (TLN 1148).

anchor_text: Do curse the gout, serpigo, and the rheum
summary: Three ailments associated with old age. Gout is a joint disease caused by uric-acid crystals, affecting the feet and knees; it was seen as the disease of the rich who ate too much. 'Serpigo' is a creeping skin disease — ringworm or a spreading rash. 'Rheum' meant excessive mucus, associated with colds, weeping eyes, and the general wet decay of old age. The Duke's point: even your own children wish you dead sooner, because your old-age ailments make life a burden to all.

A swift ambassador delivers news and comes back; a leiger stays indefinitely. Isabella is saying: you will be sent to God's court, but you will not be coming back.

anchor_text: Ay, just; perpetual durance
summary: 'Durance' means imprisonment, confinement — from Old French durance, 'hardship, captivity.' Isabella is revealing that Angelo's 'mercy' is not a pardon but a kind of living death: Claudio would be imprisoned forever, or shackled by shame and dishonour that would follow him all his life. She stresses the word 'perpetual' to underline that what Angelo offers is bondage, not freedom.

anchor_text: Would bark your honour from that trunk you bear
summary: Isabella uses a tree metaphor: 'bark' is the outer skin of a tree, and 'trunk' is its main body. To 'bark' a tree is to strip its protective outer layer, which kills it. Accepting Angelo's terms would strip Claudio's honour — his social identity, the thing that protects his worth as a person — from the body (trunk) that carries it. The image implies that honour is not merely decorative but as essential as bark is to a living tree.

anchor_text: The sense of death is most in apprehension; And the poor beetle that we tread upon In corporal sufferance finds a pang as great As when a giant dies.
summary: 'Apprehension' here means the dread or anticipatory fear of something, not the moment of experiencing it. Isabella argues that the actual pain of dying — what the body physically suffers ('corporal sufferance') — is no greater for a human being than for the beetle underfoot. What makes death terrible is the imagination of it, not the fact. She is telling Claudio that his terror is a mental event, not a measure of how bad the thing itself will be.
detail: The beetle argument is a compressed piece of Stoic reasoning: if physical pain is the same regardless of who experiences it, then death is being feared for the wrong reason. Isabella is trying to stiffen Claudio's resolve by distinguishing the idea of death (which the mind inflates into something monstrous) from the event itself. The argument fails on Claudio, who responds with one of Shakespeare's most honest expressions of mortal fear (TLN 1268-1282), precisely refusing to pretend that imagination alone makes death bad.

anchor_text: This outward-sainted deputy,-- Whose settled visage and deliberate word Nips youth i' the head, and follies doth emmew As falcon doth the fowl,--is yet a devil
summary: 'Outward-sainted' means saintly only on the outside — the appearance of holiness with none of the reality inside. 'Emmew' (or 'enmew') is a falconry term: to drive quarry into a mew (an enclosure or hiding place), as a hunting falcon drives its prey. Angelo's authority does not kill youthful impulses directly; it drives them into hiding where they fester. Isabella is exposing the gap between Angelo's sanctimonious exterior and his corrupt interior.
detail: The falconry image is precise: a falcon does not always strike its prey outright but can herd it, cutting off escape routes until the bird is cornered. Angelo's 'settled visage and deliberate word' perform a similar herding function on Vienna's youth — his cold authority does not so much reform them as suppress and conceal their impulses. Isabella uses this image to suggest his power is coercive and theatrical rather than genuinely transformative. The gap between holy appearance and devilish reality is the play's central irony, announced here before Claudio or the audience knows the full extent of Angelo's hypocrisy.
