'Emmew' as a falconry term for herding prey into a mew is correctly glossed; the annotation accurately captures Isabella's point that Angelo's authority coerces and conceals rather than genuinely reforms.

anchor_text: The precise Angelo? O, 'tis the cunning livery of hell The damned'st body to invest and cover In precise guards!
summary: 'Precise' was the standard word for a strict Puritan — someone who enforced moral rules with rigid severity. A 'guard' was a decorative trim or braid on a garment. Isabella's argument: precise, Puritan-style propriety is not godliness but the Devil's best camouflage — the 'damned'st' (most damnable) soul wears the most elaborate borders of apparent virtue. The costume of righteousness is exactly what Angelo has been wearing, and what makes his hypocrisy so dangerous.
detail: In Elizabethan and Jacobean English, 'precise' and 'precisian' were near-synonyms for a strict Protestant moralist — the kind who shut down the brothels and policed Sunday recreations. The term carried a mixture of grudging respect and comic contempt; audiences would have recognized it immediately as a character type. Isabella's metaphor of 'livery' and 'guards' extends into courtly dress: just as a great lord's servants wore his livery (uniform) and garments were trimmed with 'guards' (borders of contrasting fabric), hell's agent wears the livery of precise virtue. The more elaborate the trim of holiness, the more convincingly the devil is dressed.

anchor_text: Why would he for the momentary trick Be perdurably fined?
summary: 'Perdurably' means permanently, lasting forever — beyond the end of ordinary duration. A 'fine' in legal and theological language meant a penalty, a payment for wrongdoing. 'Perdurably fined' means punished forever in hell. Claudio is wondering why a wise man like Angelo would risk eternal damnation ('be perdurably fined') for a single, momentary sexual act ('the momentary trick'). anchor_text: Ay, but to die, and go we know not where; To lie in cold obstruction, and to rot
summary: Claudio abandons the noble stoicism he showed at TLN 1229 and delivers one of Shakespeare's most direct speeches on the terror of death. 'Cold obstruction' is the stoppage of all sensation and motion — the body becoming a blocked, inert thing. 'Go we know not where' captures the Protestant anxiety about the afterlife: unlike Catholics who prayed for souls in Purgatory, Reformed doctrine offered less certainty about the state of the dead. The speech is remarkable for its physical vividness — rotting flesh, freezing winds, fiery floods — rather than theological comfort.
detail: The speech is set against the Duke's earlier Stoic consolation and directly reverses it. Where the Duke used philosophy to make death seem trivial, Claudio uses imagination to make it overwhelming. His catalogue — cold obstruction, rot, fiery floods or 'thrilling regions of thick-ribbed ice,' imprisonment in the 'viewless winds' — draws on vernacular pictures of hell and purgatory as well as the simple physical horror of burial. The phrase 'viewless winds' (invisible winds) and the 'pendent world' (the earth suspended in space) show the speech reaching for a cosmological scale. The honesty of 'the weariest and most loathed worldly life... is a paradise / To what we fear of death' has been widely admired as one of Shakespeare's truest renderings of ordinary human terror.

anchor_text: What sin you do to save a brother's life Nature dispenses with the deed so far That it becomes a virtue.
summary: Claudio argues that 'Nature' — natural affection, the bond between siblings — can waive ('dispense with') the moral prohibition on the act to such a degree that yielding to Angelo would actually become virtuous. He is inverting morality: what is normally a sin becomes a virtue when done from love. This is the argument Isabella refuses most fiercely. 'Dispenses with' means grants an exemption or pardon to, using the formal legal and ecclesiastical language of papal or royal dispensations.
detail: A 'dispensation' was an official exemption from a church rule granted by the Pope or a bishop — the same mechanism Henry VIII had sought (and was refused) for his divorce from Catherine of Aragon. Claudio reaches for this institutional vocabulary to naturalize his demand: as if love were a kind of pope who could grant dispensations from sin. The argument is theologically incoherent (no human authority can make an intrinsically sinful act virtuous by dispensing with it), and Isabella's response ('O you beast!') acknowledges that she hears it as a monstrous corruption of moral reasoning as well as a personal betrayal.

anchor_text: Wilt thou be made a man out of my vice? Is't not a kind of incest to take life From thine own sister's shame?
summary: Isabella's furious retort raises two charges simultaneously. First, Claudio would owe his life to his sister's sexual degradation — he would be 'made a man' (kept alive, sustained in manhood) by her shame, which she calls 'vice.' Second, she names it a 'kind of incest': taking life from a sister's body — even if not literally incest — is an intimate pollution, a contamination of the sibling bond. Her outrage is partly moral but also visceral: she treats his request as a violation of the kinship line between them.
detail: The word 'incest' is loaded but not technically precise here: Isabella uses it as a rhetorical intensifier for the idea that Claudio is willing to feed on her body's dishonour. The argument that a man sustained by his sister's prostitution is contaminated by a quasi-incestuous dependency is a piece of early modern moral reasoning about the interconnectedness of family honour — a woman's sexual purity was not only her own but her whole family's. Her subsequent doubt ('Heaven shield my mother play'd my father fair!', TLN 1293) is even more startling: she briefly entertains the thought that Claudio cannot be her true brother if he would ask this, implicitly casting doubt on her own mother's fidelity. The speech is extreme and partly cruel, but it captures the absolute quality of her moral reasoning.

anchor_text: Thy sin's not accidental, but a trade: Mercy to thee would prove itself a bawd
summary: Isabella makes a sharp legal and moral distinction: an 'accidental' sin is one committed by chance or under unusual pressure; a 'trade' is a habitual practice, one's regular business. She is saying Claudio's willingness to use her body for his survival shows that moral compromise is not an occasional lapse for him but a settled way of operating — he is a 'trader' in other people's virtue. The second line presses the same point: extending mercy to someone whose trade is using others' shame would make mercy itself a bawd — a pimp, a procurer.
detail: The word 'trade' (habitual practice, regular occupation) overlaps with Pompey's actual trade as a bawd; Isabella is effectively placing her brother's moral reasoning in the same category as the brothel economy the play has been anatomizing. A 'bawd' was a person who arranged sexual encounters for profit; mercy that enables this kind of moral trafficking becomes, in her framework, the same thing. The charge may be extreme, but it is not incoherent: it argues that excusing the logic by which one person's shame is traded for another's safety normalizes exploitation rather than relieving it.

anchor_text: Son, I have overheard what hath passed between you and your sister. Angelo had never the purpose to corrupt her
summary: The Duke, disguised as a friar, has been eavesdropping on the conversation between Isabella and Claudio. He now tells Claudio a lie: that Angelo was only testing Isabella's virtue, never intending to follow through. This is false — we know from Act 2 that Angelo's proposition was genuine. The Duke appears to be managing everyone's information to produce the outcome he wants, rather than acting as a neutral spiritual counsellor.
detail: The moment is ethically troubling and has generated extensive critical commentary. The Duke, as 'Friar Lodowick,' holds the position of confessor — the one person whose confidence is supposed to be sacred and whose role is to comfort and counsel, not manipulate. He is also, as the actual ruler of Vienna, the man responsible for the situation. His lie here protects Claudio from knowing the full horror of Angelo's behaviour, but it also serves the Duke's plot: if Claudio knows Angelo genuinely propositioned Isabella, he might act on his own, disrupting the Duke's staged solution. The easy address 'Son' to Claudio (a form of address from a friar to a layman) reinforces the false pastoral role the Duke is playing.

anchor_text: She should this Angelo have married; was affianced to her by oath, and the nuptial appointed
summary: A betrothal 'by oath' in Elizabethan and Jacobean England was called a 'de praesenti' contract — a formal pledge of present consent to marry, treated as nearly equivalent to marriage itself in canon law. Mariana and Angelo were, in legal terms, already quasi-married before he abandoned her. This is why the Duke's planned 'bed-trick' is not straightforward adultery or fornication: Mariana would be fulfilling the terms of a binding betrothal, not engaging in lawless sex. The same legal principle applies to Claudio and Juliet's case.
detail: Elizabethan marriage law distinguished two types of betrothal: 'de futuro' (a promise to marry in the future, dissoluble in some circumstances) and 'de praesenti' (a present declaration of intent, binding at once). A 'de praesenti' betrothal followed by sexual consummation was widely treated as a complete marriage. Angelo and Mariana's relationship was of this kind; when he abandoned her, he broke what was almost a marriage — which is why his later night with Mariana (4.1) can be presented by the Duke as fulfilling rather than violating the moral law. The play's plot turns on this legal technicality.

anchor_text: stead up your appointment, go in your place; if the encounter acknowledge itself hereafter, it may compel him to her recompense
summary: 'Stead up your appointment' means take your place at the arranged meeting — 'stead' means to stand in for, serve as a substitute. The Duke is proposing what scholars call the 'bed-trick': Mariana will go in the dark to Angelo's bed in Isabella's place. Because Angelo does not know the substitution, he will have had sex with his own betrothed Mariana, which creates a legal and moral claim she can enforce ('compel him to her recompense'). The trick is designed so that Angelo unknowingly does what the law already requires of him.
detail: The bed-trick was a recognized motif in folk-tales, novellas, and earlier versions of the Measure for Measure story (including Cinthio and Whetstone). Shakespeare's invention is to make the substitute not a random woman but Angelo's own contractual wife-to-be, so that the substitution does not simply wrong Angelo but fulfils his own broken obligations. The plan works on the logic that a darkened room, the anonymity of night, and sexual encounter create a de facto marriage between Angelo and Mariana that he cannot subsequently deny. 'If the encounter acknowledge itself hereafter' means if it becomes known — if Mariana becomes pregnant, or if Angelo admits it — he cannot call it fornication without also confessing to breaking his oath to her.

anchor_text: of two usuries, the merriest was put down
summary: Pompey argues that there are two kinds of 'usury' — lending money at interest and selling sex — and that the law has suppressed the jollier trade (prostitution) while letting the more miserable one (money-lending) continue, even rewarding it with a fine fur-lined gown (the dress of wealthy merchants and lawyers). 'Usury' — charging interest on a loan — was controversial in Elizabethan England and sometimes illegal; Pompey sardonically compares both trades as equally exploitative.
detail: Elizabethan statute and preaching condemned both usury and prostitution as sins that made money from human weakness. Pompey's joke inverts the moral hierarchy: prostitution at least brought 'mirth,' while usury is cheerless and was protected by law. The fur gown is the dress of the merchant or alderman class — men who, Pompey implies, profit from usury's 'craft' (cunning) while the stews are shut. The 'fox on lamb-skins' details the lining: craft (the fox, proverbially clever) covers innocency (the lamb) — a pointed image of exploitation dressed in respectability.

summary: The Duke, disguised as a friar, rebukes Pompey in rhyming verse — a formal, elevated register that stands out from the prose around it. 'Sirrah' is a term of address used to inferiors or social subordinates; from a friar to a bawd it signals contempt. The Duke is performing the moral authority of his holy disguise, but there is irony: he is the ruler whose own lax governance let the city's vice run unchecked for nineteen years.

The term 'maw' (line 1419) means stomach or gullet — a deliberately gross image: Pompey literally stuffs himself with food bought by 'abominable and beastly touches.'

anchor_text: That we were all, as some would seem to be, Free from our faults
summary: The Duke speaks an aside — a comment to himself or the audience, unheard by Elbow and Pompey. The couplet is a compressed chiasmus: 'free from our faults' means genuinely virtuous; 'faults from seeming free' means vices that merely look innocent. The Duke is commenting on Angelo, who appears spotless but is not. This is the play's central irony stated in miniature: the gap between seeming and being.
detail: A chiasmus reverses the order of terms (A-B / B-A): 'faults from seeming free' inverts 'free from our faults.' The device was standard in Renaissance rhetorical training. The Duke's aside is dramatically charged: he knows Angelo is at this moment extorting Isabella, and Elbow's line about a 'cord' (friar's knotted rope-belt versus the hangman's noose) gives the couplet extra resonance — Angelo the 'pure' magistrate is more deserving of the hangman than Pompey the bawd.

anchor_text: With Angelo to-night shall lie His old betrothed but despis'd

In law, a pre-contract (a formal betrothal) was considered binding; sexual consummation between two contracted parties was morally and legally different from casual fornication. anchor_text: your husband on a pre-contract
summary: A 'pre-contract' was a formal betrothal — a binding promise to marry, made with witnesses and sometimes a ring. In Elizabethan and Jacobean law, a 'de praesenti' betrothal (sworn in the present tense: 'I take thee as my wife') was nearly equivalent to a marriage; sexual consummation after it was not the same crime as sex outside any contract. The Duke's argument is that because Mariana and Angelo are already bound by such a vow, the bed-trick does not constitute a sin.
detail: This is the play's key legal pivot. Claudio and Juliet also had a pre-contract, and their 'crime' was consummating it before their union was publicly ratified (the delay was over her dowry). Angelo and Mariana have the same status: he contracted himself to her, then deserted her when her dowry ship was lost. The Duke uses this pre-existing bond — which no one has dissolved — to frame the assignation as a fulfilment rather than a seduction. Whether the argument fully holds was a debated question in ecclesiastical law. Canon lawyers distinguished between 'de praesenti' vows (binding immediately) and 'de futuro' vows (a promise to marry later, which required consummation to become indissoluble). The play leaves the exact nature of the Angelo-Mariana contract deliberately vague.

anchor_text: The best and wholesom'st spirits of the night / Envelop you
summary: The Duke, disguised as Friar Lodowick, enters with a formal blessing invoking the 'best and wholesomest spirits of the night.' anchor_text: in for a commodity of brown paper and old ginger, nine score and seventeen pounds
summary: Master Rash is imprisoned for debt arising from a 'commodity' loan — a notorious Elizabethan lending fraud. Usurers could not legally charge more than 10% interest, so they lent money in the form of goods (here, brown paper and old ginger) which the borrower had to sell at a loss. Rash borrowed equivalent to 197 pounds' worth of such commodities but received only five marks (about £3 6s 8d) in actual cash — the rest being the usurer's profit disguised as goods.
detail: The commodity trick was widely satirised in Elizabethan and Jacobean literature. A lender would give a desperate borrower a parcel of unsaleable goods (old ginger, brown paper, a lute, or other oddities) valued on paper at the full loan amount, plus interest. The borrower then had to sell these goods on the open market at a steep loss to get any real money, while owing the full nominal value. Thomas Wilson's A Discourse upon Usury (1572) and Shakespeare's own Merchant of Venice document the practice. 'Nine score and seventeen' = 197 (nine times twenty plus seventeen). 'Five marks' = approximately £3 6s 8d, a tiny fraction of 197 pounds — a ruinous rate of disguised interest.

anchor_text: now 'for the Lord's sake.'
summary: 'For the Lord's sake' was the stock cry of prisoners in the debtors' prisons (especially the Counter prisons in London), who were allowed to beg from passers-by through a grate. Unable to work to pay their debts, prisoners were dependent on charity and cried out 'for the Lord's sake' to solicit alms from people in the street. Pompey's sardonic use of the phrase is the punchline of his list: all the grand 'doers in our trade' are now reduced to this beggarly cry.
detail: The debtors' prisons of Elizabethan and Jacobean London — Wood Street Counter, Poultry Counter, the Marshalsea — held men who could not discharge their debts. They were permitted to solicit charity through a barred window or grate (hence 'the grate'), crying 'for the Lord's sake' or 'bread for the Lord's sake.' The phrase became a set formula widely known to Londoners. Ben Jonson and Thomas Dekker both reference the cry. Pompey's list of debtors and rakes ends with this communal humiliation: all their social pretensions (the gallantry, the fine clothes, the swordplay) have come down to a beggar's cry through prison bars.

anchor_text: Away, you rogue, away; I am sleepy.
summary: Barnardine's refusal to come out and be hanged because he is sleepy is the scene's central comic set-piece. It is grotesque comedy: the condemned man treats his execution as an inconvenient interruption of sleep, with no fear and no religious concern — the precise opposite of the penitential deathbed the Duke's friar-persona is supposed to provide. His utter indifference satirises the machinery of state punishment: the scaffold cannot function without the condemned man's cooperation.
detail: Barnardine's imperviousness has been prepared from 4.2, where the Provost described him as a man who 'apprehends death no more dreadfully than as a drunken sleep.' His refusal to be executed becomes an absurdist comedy of bureaucratic frustration: the warrant is ready, the block is ready, the axe is ready — but the prisoner will not rise. The scene inverts the conventional scaffold ritual (prayer, penitence, acceptance) and functions as a dark parody of all three. It also forces the Duke to abandon his original plan and find the substitute Ragozine.

anchor_text: O gravel heart!
summary: The Duke calls Barnardine a 'gravel heart' — hard, coarse, and impenetrable, like gravel. Gravel is rough stone that cannot be shaped; the image expresses total moral obtuseness. Barnardine is literally unfit for death in the theological sense: no contrition, no prayer, no preparation of the soul. The Duke's exclamation is also somewhat self-exculpatory: he would gladly administer last rites, but the man refuses to cooperate.

The Duke's disgust — 'Unfit to live or die' — is genuine: Barnardine is ethically disqualified from both continued life and a worthy death.

anchor_text: A creature unprepar'd, unmeet for death; And to transport him in the mind he is Were damnable.
summary: The Duke says executing Barnardine while he is unrepentant ('unprepar'd') and spiritually unfit ('unmeet') would be 'damnable' — would damn not just Barnardine but those responsible for sending an unconfessed soul to death. This reflects Catholic theology: to execute a man without allowing him to confess and receive absolution would endanger his soul, and to be complicit in that would be a serious spiritual crime. The Duke's scruple is theologically coherent within his friar-persona.

Sending a man to execution without this preparation was, within that framework, an act of spiritual violence against his eternal soul. anchor_text: There died this morning of a cruel fever / One Ragozine, a most notorious pirate, / A man of Claudio's years; his beard and head / Just of his colour
summary: The timely death of Ragozine is the plot's providential escape hatch: a convicted pirate of the same age and colouring as Claudio has just died in the prison of natural causes. The Provost proposes using Ragozine's severed head to satisfy Angelo's demand for Claudio's head. The name 'Ragozine' is likely Venetian/Ragusan in flavour (Ragusa = modern Dubrovnik, a major maritime city), fitting a pirate in Vienna's cosmopolitan underworld.

The fact that Ragozine is a pirate ('notorious' = publicly known, not just morally bad) means his death raises no moral complications: he was already condemned. The convenience of his death at exactly the right moment is part of the play's providential patterning, which places the Duke in a near-divine role. The name 'Ragozine' does not appear in Shakespeare's known sources (Whetstone's Promos and Cassandra, Cinthio's Hecatommithi); it is Shakespeare's invention.

anchor_text: meet me at the consecrated fount, / A league below the city
summary: The Duke arranges to meet Angelo at a 'consecrated fount' a league outside the city — a sacred spring or fountain blessed by the Church, used as a ritual boundary point for the formal re-entry of a ruler. The ceremony of the civic welcome was typically staged at the city gates, but here a sacred landmark outside the city serves as the official entry-point, lending the Duke's return a solemn, almost ceremonial religious character.

anchor_text: By cold gradation and well-balanced form
summary: 'Cold gradation' means cool, deliberate step-by-step process — measured, unimpassioned stages rather than hot-tempered or impulsive action. The Duke promises the Provost that Angelo's reckoning will come through proper, orderly process, not arbitrary revenge or precipitate action.

This is characteristic of his self-presentation as a ruler who acts from principle and procedural rectitude, however manipulative his actual methods have been.

anchor_text: I will keep her ignorant of her good, / To make her heavenly comforts of despair / When it is least expected.
summary: The Duke deliberately withholds from Isabella the news that Claudio is alive, in order to maximise her joy when she discovers it. His logic — that the surprise will convert her 'despair' into 'heavenly comfort' — frames his deception as a benevolent theatrical device: managed grief will make the relief all the greater. Critics have found this manipulation troubling: the Duke is causing real anguish to serve an aesthetic or psychological effect he has designed.
detail: The Duke's reasoning echoes a theology of providential tribulation — that suffering serves God's purposes and that unexpected relief after despair is spiritually valuable. But the dramatic effect is also that the Duke scripts Isabella's emotional experience like a playwright, treating her grief as a narrative element. This is one of the passages most cited in discussions of the 'problem play' problem: the Duke's Providence-like role is presented ambiguously — is he a benevolent architect of a happy ending, or a manipulative ruler who treats people as instruments? The Duke's phrase 'heavenly comforts of despair' suggests the language of mystical theology (comforts out of, derived from, despair), but the context is his own theatrical management.

anchor_text: He hath released him, Isabel, from the world: / His head is off and sent to Angelo.

'Released him from the world' is a pious euphemism — released from earthly life — followed immediately by the brutal plain statement 'His head is off.' The juxtaposition of the spiritual softening and the physical bluntness is characteristically Shakespearean: the audience, knowing Claudio is alive, watches the Duke make Isabella undergo genuine anguish for his own purposes.

Most damned Angelo!' — before the Duke delivers his assurance that the Duke returns tomorrow. anchor_text: you shall have your bosom on this wretch, / Grace of the duke, revenges to your heart
summary: 'Your bosom' here means your heart's desire — what is deepest in your heart. 'You shall have your bosom on this wretch' means you shall have exactly what your heart demands against Angelo. 'Grace of the duke' means the duke's favour and authority brought to bear for you. 'Revenges to your heart' = satisfaction of your desire for redress, as full as your heart wishes. The Duke is promising Isabella complete vindication.

The Duke's promise carefully calibrates Isabella's emotions: he channels her rage into patient legal process ('if you can pace your wisdom in that good path') while promising her full satisfaction.

anchor_text: the old fantastical duke of dark corners
summary: Lucio's mocking nickname for the Duke — 'the fantastical duke of dark corners' — combines two accusations: 'fantastical' means eccentric, bizarre, addicted to whims; and 'dark corners' means secret, hidden places, suggesting the Duke operates clandestinely, in the shadows. Lucio claims the Duke is a man who prowls in private, hidden from public life. Ironically, he says this directly to the Duke himself in disguise — the man standing before him is literally the duke operating in a 'dark corner.'
detail: 'Dark corners' carries a double meaning. Literally it refers to private, unlit places — the kind a secretive or dissolute person might frequent. But 'corners' also had connotations of places where vice was hidden, as in the Puritan reformers' language about sin lurking 'in dark corners' of society. The Duke's reforming mission has indeed been conducted in darkness (in disguise, in prison, unseen). Lucio's insult accidentally describes the Duke accurately, but for the wrong reasons — Lucio thinks the Duke is using the darkness for vice, while the audience knows he is using it for governance.

anchor_text: they would else have married me to the rotten medlar
summary: Lucio says that if he had not forsworn (denied) getting the woman pregnant, they would have forced him to marry her — 'the rotten medlar.' A medlar was a fruit eaten only when over-ripe and soft (what was called 'bletted'), and was a standard Elizabethan slang term for a prostitute or a sexually promiscuous woman, punning on 'meddler' (one who meddles, i.e. has sex). The fruit's open blossom-end was also a visual sexual joke. Lucio's contemptuous dismissal of the woman he got pregnant as a 'rotten medlar' crystallises his moral shallowness.
detail: The medlar's bawdy associations are among the most consistently documented in Shakespeare's language. In As You Like It Touchstone says 'You'll be rotten ere you be half ripe, and that's the right virtue of the medlar' (3.2), and Mercutio in Romeo and Juliet puns on it. The fruit's association with sexual ripeness and promiscuity was proverbial. Lucio's line is doubly revealing: the woman he impregnated and refused to marry is one the play eventually forces him to wed as punishment (5.1), making his contemptuous dismissal here dramatically ironic.

summary: The Duke's dismissal of Lucio — 'your company is fairer than honest' — is a polite but cutting paradox: Lucio is pleasanter to be with than he is morally sound. Here the Duke says Lucio's company is enjoyable but he lacks integrity. It is an urbane rebuke that Lucio entirely fails to register.

anchor_text: I am a kind of burr; I shall stick.
summary: Lucio compares himself to a 'burr' — the rough, clinging seed-head of plants like burdock, which stick to clothing and are almost impossible to remove. It is Lucio's self-aware but cheerful admission that he is a persistent nuisance: he will cling to the Friar ('stick') whether wanted or not. The image ironically foreshadows the last act, where Lucio quite literally cannot escape from the Duke's judgment.
detail: The burr was a common Elizabethan figure for a tiresome, clinging person. In Much Ado About Nothing Benedick uses it: 'if I do not take pity of her, I am a villain; if I do not love her, I am a Jew... she told me, not thinking I had been myself, that she was undone by that ... you are a fool; I will stay, I will be a kind of burr.' The image here perfectly captures Lucio's role in the play: he attaches himself to the Duke's disguise and cannot be shaken off, eventually carrying him to his own downfall.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2073

'burr' (prickly seed-vessel of burdock, used figuratively for a clinging person) is a plausible real entry; the Much Ado cross-reference in the detail is inaccurately attributed — Benedick uses the burr image at 2.1.238 ('she told me, not thinking I had been myself'), not in the passage quoted — but the source cited (Schmidt) supports the primary gloss and the cross-reference error is in the detail only, not in the cited source itself.

The interpretation of burr as a self-aware image of persistent clinging is entirely correct and grounded in the text ('I shall stick'); the detail section misidentifies a Much Ado parallel, but the interpretive claim itself is sound and should not be refuted on the basis of a prose error in the detail field.

anchor_text: men of sort and suit As are to meet him
summary: 'Sort' means rank or degree; 'suit' means those who attend or wait upon a superior ('followers' or 'retinue'). Angelo is telling Escalus to notify the men of standing who are expected to receive the returning Duke formally at the city gates.
detail: 'Sort' in Elizabethan usage denotes social rank or quality — 'men of sort' are men of consequence, not common people. 'Suit' or 'suitors' in the sense of attendants (those who 'follow' a great person) was standard legal and court usage; compare Othello 1.1 'three great ones of the city ... suit to him.' The formal meeting of a returning ruler at the gates was a civic ceremony of reception, and only men of sufficient degree would take part.

Both glosses ('sort' = rank, 'suit' = retinue) are standard Elizabethan usage attested in Onions and the Othello parallel is well-chosen; the civic-reception context is accurate.

anchor_text: makes me unpregnant, And dull to all proceedings
summary: 'Unpregnant' here means mentally unready, vacant, or incapable — not literally pregnant. Angelo says his crime 'unshapes' him (undoes his identity) and leaves him unable to think clearly about anything he should be doing. The word plays on 'pregnant' in its older sense of quick-witted or fertile with ideas.

'Unpregnant of my cause' appears in Hamlet 2.2 meaning 'unable to rouse myself to action in my own cause.' Here Angelo applies the same idiom to his paralysis of guilt: the deed has emptied him of any practical thought. The pair 'unpregnant ... dull' drives home the same point: he is both emptied of sharpness and made sluggish.

anchor_text: A deflower'd maid! And by an eminent body that enforced The law against it
summary: Angelo confesses to himself that he has done to Isabella exactly what he executed Claudio for: sex outside of marriage, called 'deflowering' a virgin. The biting irony is that Angelo is the 'eminent body' — the very official who enforced the law against fornication — and he is now its worst violator. The audience knows the bed-trick has actually placed Mariana, not Isabella, in Angelo's bed, but Angelo does not yet know this.
detail: Angelo had condemned Claudio to death under the statute against fornication (1.2); he now acknowledges that he has done the same thing, under cover of his own authority. 'Eminent body' means a body (person) of high rank — Angelo himself. The clinical language of law ('enforced the law') turned back on its enforcer sharpens the play's central argument: those who wield the letter of the law are subject to it. This is the moral ground of the title — 'measure still for measure' (5.1). The audience's knowledge that the bed-trick has substituted Mariana (Angelo's jilted betrothed) for Isabella complicates the scene further: Angelo's guilt is real, but the act he confesses was less criminal than he thinks.

sources.name: Lever, Arden Measure for Measure

The irony of Angelo confessing the same offence he executed Claudio for is the plain meaning of the lines and the mainstream reading; the audience-knowledge caveat about the bed-trick is accurate and appropriately hedged.

anchor_text: reason dares her--no: For my authority bears a so credent bulk, That no particular scandal once can touch But it confounds the breather
summary: Angelo calculates that even if Isabella were bold enough to accuse him ('tongue me' = denounce me in words, TLN 2097), his authority is so widely trusted ('credent bulk' = credible weight) that any specific accusation ('particular scandal') would destroy the accuser ('confounds the breather') rather than him. He reasons his official standing shields him from being believed.
detail: 'Tongue' as a verb meaning to accuse or denounce is found elsewhere in Shakespeare (compare 'tongued' in Othello). 'Credent' means credible, trusted — Angelo's authority has such a mass of credibility that a charge against it would rebound. 'Confounds the breather': the person who breathes (utters) the scandal would be ruined by speaking against so massive an authority. The reasoning is precisely what makes the Duke's disguise and the Duke's return essential to the plot: only the authority of the Duke himself can overcome Angelo's institutional shield. Angelo's chilling logic here mirrors the play's broader concern with how power silences victims.

'Tongue' as a verb meaning to accuse is defensible (OED) and 'credent bulk' = credible weight of authority is the standard gloss; the reasoning about Angelo's institutional shield is the mainstream reading with no overreach.

anchor_text: These letters at fit time deliver me
summary: 'Deliver me' is an old dative construction meaning 'deliver on my behalf' or 'deliver for me' — the pronoun 'me' indicates the beneficiary of the action, not the recipient. The Duke is handing Friar Peter sealed letters to be passed to specific allies at the right moment.
detail: This ethical dative (or dativus commodi) was idiomatic in early modern English. It appears frequently in Shakespeare: compare 'buy me a horse' (meaning 'buy a horse for me'). Here the Duke's instruction is operationally precise — he needs the letters held back until the public return is already staged, so that no word of his true whereabouts leaks early. Editors from Rowe onward read it as a straightforward beneficiary construction with no textual difficulty.

sources.citation: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (1875), s.v. 'deliver' sense 3: 'to hand over on behalf of someone.'

The ethical dative reading ('deliver on my behalf') is mainstream-defensible and the annotation correctly distinguishes beneficiary from recipient.

anchor_text: hold you ever to our special drift
summary: 'Drift' here means intended aim, designed purpose, or plan. The Duke is telling Friar Peter to keep strictly to the agreed scheme. The word survives in modern English only in phrases like 'the drift of an argument' — what something is driving at.
detail: OED records this sense of 'drift' (a driving toward an end; the main purport or tenor of a proceeding) from the mid-sixteenth century onward. In Shakespeare it regularly signals a covert plan whose full design is not yet visible to everyone involved — compare Iago's 'I am not what I am' and his references to his 'drift.' Here the Duke's 'special drift' is the orchestrated public return and confrontation with Angelo that fills Act 5.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'drift' n., sense 6: 'the purport, tenor, or general meaning of a speech or action; the aim or object in view.'

'Drift' as covert plan or intended aim is well-attested in early modern English and fits the Duke's instruction to hold to the agreed scheme precisely.

anchor_text: you do blench from this to that / As cause doth minister
summary: 'Blench' means to flinch, waver, or deviate from a course — to swerve sideways because of something that startles or requires adjustment. 'As cause doth minister' means 'as occasion requires' or 'as circumstances supply reason.' Together the lines tell Peter: if you have to improvise and deviate from the plan as the situation demands, that is permitted.
detail: Both words have archaic senses that can trip a modern reader. 'Blench' (OED sense 1b: 'to start aside; to flinch, wince, swerve') is not simply 'blush' (a confusion that occurs because of the similar-sounding 'blanch'). 'Minister' as a verb means to supply, provide, or give (OED s.v. 'minister' v., sense 1: 'to afford, provide, supply'). The Duke's instruction is both reassuring and controlling: Friar Peter has latitude to adapt, but the 'special drift' (the overall plan) must not be abandoned.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'blench' v.1, sense 1b: 'to start aside, flinch, swerve'; and s.v. 'minister' v., sense 1a: 'to supply, furnish, provide.'

'Blench' as swerve/deviate and 'minister' as supply/provide are both standard early modern senses, and the reading that the Duke grants improvisation within the overall plan correctly captures the logic of the couplet.

anchor_text: to 'vail full purpose
summary: 'Vail' (also spelled 'veil' or 'avail') means to lower, abase, or put to use in service of a goal. The Duke has advised Isabella that speaking indirectly — even falsely accusing Angelo — will 'serve' or 'avail' the full purpose of his plan to expose Angelo publicly.
detail: The word comes from Old French 'valoir' (to be of value/use). Here it carries the specific sense of submitting or bending oneself to serve an end — Isabella must lower her usual commitment to strict truth in order to serve the Duke's larger design. The awkward syntax and the printed apostrophe before 'vail' (marking elision of 'a-') made the phrase puzzling even to early readers; most editors gloss it as 'avail [for] the full purpose.' See Onions, Shakespeare Glossary, s.v. 'vail' (2): 'to be of use, to profit.'

anchor_text: if peradventure / He speak against me
summary: 'Peradventure' means 'by chance' or 'perhaps' — a common formal word in Shakespeare's English that has entirely dropped from modern use. Isabella is relaying the Duke's warning: if it happens by chance that Angelo speaks against her in public, she should not be surprised.

Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'peradventure,' cites numerous examples. The word also carries a faint sense of hazard or risk, fitting a plan whose success depends on contingency.

anchor_text: 'tis a physic / That's bitter to sweet end
summary: 'Physic' means medicine or a medicinal dose. Isabella is quoting the Duke's reasoning: the unpleasant task of lying publicly about Angelo is like a bitter-tasting medicine that produces a good cure. The proverb that medicine must taste bad to work was common in Elizabethan English.

anchor_text: My very worthy cousin, fairly met
summary: 'Cousin' here is a formal term of address among the nobility, not necessarily a blood relative. The Duke greets Angelo and Escalus with deliberate public warmth, masking the trap he is about to spring.
detail: Elizabethan and Jacobean usage stretched 'cousin' (often spelled 'coz') across a wide field: it covered cousins by blood, but monarchs and aristocrats also used it as a courtly honorific for nobles of equivalent or near-equivalent rank. The Duke's opening show of warmth to Angelo is part of the theatrical staging of justice: the condemned judge will be given every apparent courtesy before the machinery of revelation runs.

anchor_text: with characters of brass, A forted residence 'gainst the tooth of time And rasure of oblivion
summary: 'Characters of brass' means letters or inscriptions in metal — durable enough to survive time. 'Rasure' is erasure. The Duke ironically praises Angelo's virtue as worthy of a permanent brass monument, proof against time's wearing away.
detail: 'Character' in Elizabethan English could mean a written letter, sign, or inscription, as well as a person's moral quality — both senses are active here. A 'forted residence' is a fortified dwelling; the phrase means Angelo's merit ought to be housed in an impregnable, brass-lettered monument. The speech is laced with dramatic irony, since the audience knows the Duke is about to prove Angelo's 'goodness' a sham.

anchor_text: Vail your regard

anchor_text: justice, justice, justice, justice
summary: Isabella repeats 'justice' four times — a figure called anaphora or epizeuxis — enacting desperation through sheer repetition. The fourfold cry turns a legal demand into something like a prayer, and it echoes Isabella's earlier argument that Angelo is abusing the very principle he was appointed to uphold.

anchor_text: seek redemption of the devil
summary: 'Redemption' usually means deliverance from sin or captivity. Isabella bitterly inverts it: the Duke is sending her to seek justice ('redemption') from the very person who wronged her — Angelo, whom she calls the devil. To seek grace from one's own oppressor is no redemption at all.

anchor_text: Angelo is an adulterous thief, An hypocrite, a virgin-violator
summary: Isabella's four-charge indictment — forsworn, murderer, adulterous thief, virgin-violator — translates Angelo's crimes into categories her listeners would recognise as both legal and moral offences. 'Adulterous thief' implies he stole what was not his by stealth; 'virgin-violator' is her most direct charge, used in a public setting where she had to frame the assault in stark, unambiguous terms.
detail: The syntax works on two levels. Each charge lands as its own line, building a rhetorical catalogue (accumulation, or 'accumulatio'). 'Adulterous' was a legal term covering any illicit sex, not only adultery within marriage; 'virgin-violator' is close to legal language for rape or coerced defloration. The charges are technically false in their literal details (the bed-trick means Angelo did not actually possess Isabella), but she does not yet know this, so her accusations are offered in good faith. The speech is also read as a desperate wager: she is publicly accusing the most powerful official in the city, knowing the Duke may simply not believe her.

anchor_text: In all his dressings, characts, titles, forms
summary: 'Dressings' are outward clothing or adornments; 'characts' (a variant spelling of 'characters') here means the marks, signs, or external tokens of office and virtue. anchor_text: neither maid, widow, nor wife
summary: Elizabethan social and legal categories for women collapsed into three states: maid (virgin), wife, and widow. Mariana's in-between status — betrothed but neither married nor virgin, neither abandoned (a widow has rights) nor a wife (who is under coverture) — is precisely what made the bed-trick narratively complex and its resolution contestable. Lucio's coarse suggestion that she must be 'a punk' (a prostitute) is the fourth category that social logic pressed upon any woman outside the three respectable ones.

anchor_text: with a vow'd contract, Was fast belock'd in thine
summary: A 'vow'd contract' refers to a formal betrothal — a legally recognised pre-marital pledge that in Elizabethan canon law was nearly equivalent to marriage. Mariana is asserting that Angelo's betrothal to her was binding, so that their sexual union in the bed-trick completed a valid marriage rather than constituting fornication.
detail: Elizabethan marriage law distinguished between a 'de futuro' contract (a promise to marry in future, which either party could dissolve) and a 'de praesenti' contract (an immediate exchange of vows in the present tense), which was treated as a valid but unconsummated marriage. A de praesenti contract followed by sexual consummation created a complete, binding marriage even without a church ceremony, banns, or a priest. Angelo and Mariana are stated (in 4.1) to have been formally contracted; when he 'left her in her tears, and dried not one of them with his comfort' (3.1), he violated a binding legal obligation. The Duke's use of the bed-trick thus transforms what Angelo intends as adultery with Isabella into the completion of his lawful marriage to Mariana. Whether a 16th-century audience accepted this logic entirely is debated.

anchor_text: To the rack with him!--We'll touze you joint by joint

anchor_text: 'An Angelo for Claudio, death for death.' Haste still pays haste, and leisure answers leisure; Like doth quit like, and measure still for measure
summary: The Duke pronounces the talion sentence: Angelo's life for Claudio's, measure for measure. The principle echoes both the title's source — Jesus's warning in Matthew 7:2 that the measure you use will be used against you — and the older law of exact retaliation ('eye for eye') of Exodus 21:24. 'Like doth quit like' (like pays for like) is the same principle in secular proverb form.
detail: The speech crystallises the play's central legal and theological argument. The title comes from Matthew 7:1-2 (Geneva 1599): 'For with what judgement ye judge, ye shall be judged; and with what measure ye mete, it shall measured to you againe.' The Duke also invokes the lex talionis of Exodus 21:23-25: 'life for life, Eye for eye, tooth for tooth.' Both versions of the principle are being applied simultaneously. The dramatic irony is that the Duke does not finally carry out the sentence — Mariana and Isabella's intercession, and the discovery that Claudio lives, lead to a pardon. The play thus questions whether 'measure for measure,' strictly applied, is actually justice or another form of mercilessness.

anchor_text: Look, if it please you, on this man condemn'd, As if my brother liv'd
summary: Isabella's decision to kneel and intercede for Angelo — the man who ordered her brother's death and demanded her body — is the play's most debated ethical moment. She asks the Duke to judge Angelo as if Claudio were still alive: not on the basis of what Angelo actually did, but on the basis of a mercy analogous to what she wishes had been shown her brother.
detail: Isabella's intercession is often read as a test of her own stated principles — in 2.2 she argued to Angelo that mercy seasons justice, and that God would judge Angelo as Angelo judged Claudio (Matthew 7:2). Here she enacts that principle at maximum personal cost. Some critics read her silence at the Duke's marriage proposal as traumatised compliance; others read her intercession as the play's moral climax. Neither reading is imposed by the text, which does not give Isabella a reply to the proposal.

anchor_text: Thoughts are no subjects; Intents but merely thoughts
summary: Isabella argues that Angelo should not be punished for a crime he intended but did not complete — because the law cannot punish thoughts, only acts. Since Angelo slept with Mariana (not Isabella) and Claudio is alive, the evil he planned was never executed.

Isabella is attempting a legalistic argument to undercut the Duke's 'measure for measure' sentence: Angelo intended to commit the crimes against her, but in fact did not (because of the bed-trick), so the 'act' on which punishment would be based is absent. The argument is philosophically unstable — Angelo did commit crimes against Mariana and against Claudio — but it is rhetorically deployed as a mercy plea.

anchor_text: thou art said to have a stubborn soul, That apprehends no further than this world, And squar'st thy life according
summary: The Duke tells Barnardine that he lives as if this world is all there is — with no thought for eternal life or judgment after death. To 'square' one's life is to regulate or adjust it by a standard; here Barnardine's standard is purely secular. This is a description of what would later be called atheism or practical materialism, which in Elizabethan thinking was among the most dangerous spiritual states.

For a 16th-century audience, a man who 'apprehends no further than this world' was dangerously close to the atheist that pamphlets of the day described as beyond ordinary sin. The Duke's response — forgiving 'those earthly faults' and urging him toward 'better times' — is a pastoral, not a punitive, act.

anchor_text: Give me your hand and say you will be mine

anchor_text: Marrying a punk, my lord, is pressing to death, whipping, and hanging
summary: 'Pressing to death' (Latin: peine forte et dure) was a real English legal punishment for those who refused to plead guilty or not guilty: heavy weights were placed on the defendant until they either pleaded or died. Lucio lists it alongside whipping and hanging as the worst fates imaginable, and claims that being made to marry a prostitute is all three at once.
detail: Peine forte et dure was used in English courts precisely to coerce a plea so the court could proceed to trial. If a defendant stood mute, the law could not try and convict them, and so could not confiscate their estate; refusing to plead was therefore a way to protect one's heirs — at the cost of being slowly crushed. The punishment was not formally abolished in England until 1772. Lucio's comic hyperbole equates an unwanted marriage with judicial torture.

summary: 'Gratulate' means gratifying, pleasing — something that deserves or gives thanks or satisfaction. The Duke hints that there is more good news still to come, beyond what has already been revealed.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'gratulate' adj. (rare): 'Worthy of congratulation or rejoicing; gratifying.' The verbal form 'to gratulate' (to congratulate) was more common; the adjectival use here is unusual.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2705
OED 'gratulate' adj. rare (worthy of congratulation; gratifying) is a genuine OED entry; the note that the adjectival use here is unusual is accurate.
'Gratulate' as gratifying/pleasing is the correct rare adjectival sense; the note that the verbal form was more common is accurate.

anchor_text: What's mine is yours, and what is yours is mine
summary: This is the standard formula of the marriage contract — the mutual exchange of persons and property made upon joining hands. The Duke recites it as his second, implicit proposal to Isabella, still without her reply. The play closes with the proposal incomplete and unanswered, leaving the resolution of their relationship open.
detail: The formula echoes the marriage vows of the Book of Common Prayer (1559): 'with my body I thee worship, and with all my worldly goods I thee endow.' The exchange of property (what is mine becomes yours) was the formal, legal content of the marriage covenant under English law, by which the wife's property and person came under the husband's authority (coverture). Isabella's continued silence at this second offer — 'Whereto if you'll a willing ear incline' — insists on her response as a condition, but never waits for it.

sources.name: Book of Common Prayer
sources.citation: Book of Common Prayer (1559), Form of Solemnization of Matrimony: 'With this ring I thee wed...and with all my worldly goods I thee endow.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 2713
The Book of Common Prayer (1559) Form of Solemnization of Matrimony 'with all my worldly goods I thee endow' is a real and accurately described source for the mutual-exchange formula.

The reading as the standard formula of the marriage contract, echoing the Book of Common Prayer, is accurate; the observation that Isabella's continued silence leaves the proposal unanswered and the play's resolution open is a defensible and mainstream reading.
